The expenses and commitments incurred by an authorised agency for the collection and dissemination of information related to national security interests Contingent Liability A potential liability that may occur depending on the outcome of an uncertain future event. Domestic Arrears Domestic arrears refer to short-term debts incurred by Governments against unpaid procurement invoices for supply of goods and services during the financial year External Debt Portion of a country's debt that was borrowed from foreign lenders including commercial banks, Governments or international financial institutions. Garnishee order A form of enforcing a judgment debt against a creditor to recover money. Nugatory Expenditure Expenditure that does not achieve any result Off-budget financing Off-budget refers to expenditure that is not funded through the budget Recruitment Refers to the process of attracting, screening, selecting, and on boarding a qualified person for a job, provided by an employer in another territory and the preparation for their departure Revolving Fund A fund that is continually replenished as withdrawals are made xviii Foreword In accordance with the mandate enshrined in Article 163 of the 1995 Constitution of the Republic of Uganda, and further amplified in Sections 12 and 18 of the National Audit Act, Cap 170, I hereby present the Annual Audit Report on the Consolidated Financial Statements of the Government of Uganda, as well as the Financial Performance of Public Corporations and State Enterprises. During the audit year ended 31st December 2025, I audited 182 Ministries, Departments, and Agencies (MDAs), 85 Public Corporations and State Enterprises, 181 Projects, as well as 145 Districts and Cities. In addition, I finalized 4,529 audits of Lower Local Governments and 1,228 Secondary Schools and Tertiary Institutions. Furthermore, I conducted two thematic audits focusing on Management of Procurement and implementation of the Parish Development Model. My Office’s commitment to undertaking audits that add value to society in view of stakeholder needs and emerging issues is unwavering. In this regard, I undertook 44 Special Audits and Investigations, 24 Value for Money Audits, and 6 Engineering Audits. While individual reports for these audits were issued, summaries can also be found in the respective entity/project Combined Audit Reports. As a forward-looking institution, the Office finalized a new strategic plan covering the period 2025-2030, which was approved by the National Planning Authority. Significantly, our new strategic plan was prepared in accordance with the Balanced Scorecard Framework. It emphasizes four themes, namely: service excellence, good governance, strategic partnerships, and innovation excellence. Through these themes, my office aims to consolidate its role as a model Supreme Audit Institution that not only contributes to enhancing public sector accountability and transparency but also adds value to society. I would like to express my appreciation to the Rt. Hon. Speaker of Parliament, the Rt. Hon deputy Speaker of Parliament and to Parliament as a whole, particularly the Finance Committee and the Accountability Committees, for their continued support, insights and constructive ideas aimed at enhancing the quality of my audit reports. I am equally committed to supporting the Parliamentary oversight Committees during the discussions of findings in the audit reports. I also extend my heartfelt gratitude to all stakeholders for the invaluable support throughout the audit year, that enabled me to deliver on the mandate. Special mention goes to my staff, who worked tirelessly to ensure that this report is produced within the statutory timeline. I am deeply grateful for their resilience and professionalism. Together, let us continue striving for greater accountability and transparency in the management of public resources for the benefit of our nation. Edward Akol AUDITOR GENERAL KAMPALA 31st December, 2025 1 INTRODUCTION Mandate In accordance with Article 163(3) of the 1995 Constitution of the Republic of Uganda, Sections 12 and 18 of the National Audit Act (NAA), Cap 170, and the Public Finance Management Act (PFMA), Cap 171, I am required to audit and report on the public accounts of Uganda and all public offices, including the Courts, Central and Local Government Administrations, Universities, Public Institutions of like nature and any Public Corporations or other bodies established by Acts of Parliament. Section 12(b) of the NAA, requires my office to perform a range of audits, including Financial, Value for Money, Engineering, Information Systems, Special, Government Investment Procurements, Treasury Memoranda, Gender and Environment audits, as well as audits related to any project or activity involving public funds. Additionally, Classified Expenditure audits are conducted to ensure the transparency and proper use of public resources. In compliance with Article 163(4) of the 1995 Constitution of the Republic of Uganda, I am required to audit and submit accounts to Parliament annually for the year immediately preceding. This report is submitted in compliance with the constitutional provision. Contents of the Report During the period January to December 2025, I undertook various audit types in line with my mandate and the results are as follows; (i) A report and Opinion on the Government of Uganda Consolidated Financial Statements of the Government of the Republic of Uganda for the financial year ended 30th June 2025. (ii) A review of the Consolidated Summary Statement of Financial Performance of Public Corporations and State Enterprises for the financial year ended 30th June 2025. (iii) A summary of audit results from performance evaluation of Ministries, Departments, Agencies, Commissions, Statutory Corporations and Local Governments. (iv) A summary of audit results from audit of compliance with relevant regulatory frameworks. These included Management of Procurement and the Parish Development Model (PDM). (v) A summary of audit findings from other specialized audits, Value for Money Audits, Special Audits, IT and Engineering Audits, conducted during the year. (vi) Status of implementation of the Treasury Memoranda. 2 Developments during the audit year a) Strategic Plan 2026-2030 In the Audit Year, the Office of the Auditor General (OAG) developed a new Strategic Plan, covering the period 2025-2030, which was approved by the National Planning Authority (NPA). The Strategic Plan sets a clear direction for the OAG and reaffirms our commitment to delivering high-quality audits, strengthening public accountability, and safeguarding public resources to improve service delivery. The Strategic Plan is anchored in the Balanced Scorecard Framework, which helps us ensure clarity, balance, and measurable indicators and targets. By adopting the Balanced Scorecard Framework, the OAG seeks to ensure a holistic view of its performance across four critical perspectives, namely; i) Citizen and Stakeholder Perspective: This perspective emphasizes the importance of delivering tangible value to citizens and stakeholders. The focus will be on understanding needs and expectations, ensuring that audits lead to improvements in public services that resonate with the community. ii) Financial Stewardship Perspective: Here, the OAG underlines its commitment to responsible management of resources. This entails not just maintaining fiscal discipline but also promoting transparency and accountability in the use of public funds. iii) Internal Processes Perspective: Continuous improvement in operational processes is vital for achieving efficiency and effectiveness. The OAG will explore innovative approaches and optimize workflows to enhance audit practices and broaden its impact. iv) Organisational Capacity Perspective: Recognizing that people and systems are key to success, the OAG aims to nurture its workforce and invest in capabilities. This perspective prioritizes professional development, training, and the adoption of relevant technologies to empower staff. By focusing on these four perspectives, the OAG aims to consolidate its role as a leading Supreme Audit Institution, fostering accountability and transparency within the public sector while delivering meaningful contributions to societal welfare. The commitment to measurable indicators and targets will further enable the organization to assess its progress and make necessary adjustments to ensure that its strategic goals are met effectively. 3 b) Audit of Lower Local Government, Schools & Tertiary Institutions A key milestone of audit of backlogs in the Lower Local Governments (LLGs), Town Councils, Secondary Schools and Tertiary Institutions was achieved during the audit year. This totalled to 5,529, comprising; i) 3,872 Reports for Sub-counties for the years 2021/22, 2022/23 and 2023/24 ii) 568 Reports for Town Councils for the year 2023/24 iii) 89 Municipal Divisions for the year 2023/24 v) 1,228 Reports for Secondary Schools/Tertiary Institutions for the years 2022/23 and 2023/24 or academic years 2023 and 2024 respectively. The individual reports were issued separately and a summary of cross cutting findings are included in Part V of this Report. HON. SPEAKER OF PARLIAMENT Opinion I have audited the Consolidated Financial Statements of the Government of the Republic Uganda, for the financial year ended 30th June 2025, which comprise the Statement of Financial Position as at 30th June 2025, the Statement of Financial Performance, the Statement of Changes in Equity, and the Statement of Cash Flows, together with other accompanying statements for the year then ended, and notes to the financial statements, including a summary of significant accounting policies. In my opinion, the Consolidated Financial Statements of the Government of the Republic of Uganda for the financial year ended 30th June 2025 are prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with Section 49 of the Public Finance Management Act (PFMA), Cap 171, and the Financial Reporting Guide, 2024, as issued by the Accountant General. Basis of Opinion I conducted my audit in accordance with the International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions (ISSAIs). My responsibilities under those standards are further described in the Auditor's Responsibilities for the Audit of the Financial Statements section of my report. I am independent of the Government in accordance with the 1995 Constitution of the Republic of Uganda, the National Audit Act, Cap 170, the International Organization of Supreme Audit Institutions (INTOSAI) Code of Ethics, the International Ethics Standards Board for Accountants Code of Ethics for Professional Accountants (Parts A and B) (IESBA Code), and other independence requirements applicable to performing audits of Financial Statements in Uganda. I have fulfilled my other ethical responsibilities in accordance with the IESBA Code and in accordance with other ethical requirements applicable to performing audits in Uganda. I believe that the audit evidence I have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for my opinion. Key Audit Matters Key audit matters are those matters that, in my professional judgment, are of most significance in my audit of the financial statements of the current period. I have determined that there are no key audit matters to communicate in my report. Emphasis of Matter Without qualifying my opinion, I draw attention to the following matters disclosed in the financial statements; 6 1.1 Assets Valuation I draw your attention to the Government’s reported value of property, plant and equipment worth UGX.51.2Tn disclosed in Note 24 to the financial statements. I noted that the assets being depreciated include those capitalised for the first time in FY2023/24 at estimates and/or historical values, as guided by the Accountant General. However, no professional valuation has been undertaken to date. This implies that the carrying amounts of non-current assets may not fully reflect their fair value. The Accounting Officer disclosed in his commentary, that the valuation and management of historical assets are being carried out systematically to align with full adoption of Accrual accounting across all votes, and this process is ongoing and expected to be completed by the end of FY 2025/2026, as guided by the Accountant General, to achieve fair presentation. Recommendation I advised the Accountant General to expedite the valuation of assets across Government to ensure accurate reporting, transparency, and alignment with best practices in public-sector financial management. 1.2 Trend of Payables Reported in the statement of financial position is a payables balance of UGX.8.4Tn. This reduced by UGX.5.4Tn from UGX.13.8Tn reported last year. The significant reduction in domestic arrears was due to a conversion of a temporary advance from BoU into long-term debt. UGX.7.78Tn was converted from BoU reimbursable into Treasury Bonds payable over 10 years. If this figure is eliminated, the trend of payables still moved upwards by UGX.2.36Tn despite payment of UGX0.265Tn in the year under review. The upward trend is attributed to the failed enforcement of the commitment control system and inadequate record-keeping. Recommendation I advised the Government to further enforce the commitment control system to avoid the accumulation of arrears. In addition, the Government Accounting System should be used to centrally record any commitment for which payment is not made by the close of the financial year. 1.3 Change in Revenue Recognition Policy I noted that for the period under review, URA reported gross revenue collections of UGX.32.357Tn and net revenue collections of UGX.31.635Tn as shown below; 7 Table 4: Status of revenue collections Item Amount (UGX Tn) Gross Collections 32.357 Less Refunds 0.722 Net Collections 31.635 Source: URA financials Included in the net tax collections is accrued revenue of UGX 0.868Tn expected from the Government. New guidance requires tax revenue from the Government in respect of investment subsidies to be recognised when earned. This is a departure from previous treatment, where Tax revenue was only recognised when received. The new guidance implies that all taxes to be paid by the Government on behalf of selected companies will be recognized as revenue by URA when earned rather than when received. The Accounting Officer stated that the Liability is recognized in MoFPED (Vote 008) Financial Statements and as revenue (cash in transit) in URA financial Statements, and going forward, the accounting policies for revenue recognition of intra- government transactions will be adjusted accordingly to clarify such transactions. Recommendation I advised the Accountant General to include this treatment in the Reporting Guidelines for 2026. Other Information The Accounting Officer is responsible for the other information. The other information comprises the statement of responsibilities, a statement from the Hon. Minister of Finance, Planning and Economic Development, a statement from the Secretary to the Treasury, a statement from the Accountant General and other supplementary information. The other information does not include the financial statements and my auditors' report thereon. My opinion on the financial statements does not cover the other information, and I do not express an audit opinion or any form of assurance conclusion thereon. In connection with my audit of the financial statements, my responsibility is to read the other information and, in doing so, consider whether the other information is materially consistent with the financial statements or my knowledge obtained in the audit, or otherwise appears to be materially misstated. If, based on the work I have performed, I conclude that there is a material misstatement of this other information, I am required to report that fact. I have nothing to report in this regard. Management’s Responsibility for the Financial Statements Under Article 164 of the 1995 Constitution of the Republic of Uganda and Section 43 of the Public Finance Management Act, Cap 171, the Accounting Officer is accountable to Parliament for the funds and resources of the Government. 8 The Accountant General is also responsible for the preparation of financial statements in accordance with the requirements of the Public Finance Management Act, Cap 171, and for such internal controls as the Accountant General determines are necessary to enable the preparation of financial statements that are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error. In preparing the financial statements, the Accountant General is responsible for assessing the Government’s ability to continue delivering its mandate, disclosing, as applicable, matters related to affecting the delivery of the mandate of the Government of Uganda and using the Financial Reporting Guide 2024, unless the Accountant General has a realistic alternative to the contrary. The Accountant General is responsible for overseeing the Government's financial reporting process. Auditor's Responsibilities for the Audit of the Financial Statements My objectives are to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements as a whole are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, and to issue an auditor's report that includes my opinion. Reasonable assurance is a high level of assurance, but is not a guarantee that an audit conducted in accordance with ISSAIs will always detect a material misstatement when it exists. Misstatements can arise from fraud or error and are considered material if, individually or in aggregate, they could reasonably be expected to influence the economic decisions of users, taken on the basis of these financial statements. As part of an audit in accordance with ISSAIs, I exercise professional judgement and maintain professional skepticism throughout the audit. I also;  Identify and assess the risks of material misstatement of the financial statements, whether due to fraud or error, design and perform audit procedures responsive to those risks, and obtain audit evidence that is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for my opinion. The risk of not detecting a material misstatement resulting from fraud is higher than for one resulting from error, as fraud may involve collusion, forgery, intentional omissions, misrepresentations, or the override of internal control.  Obtain an understanding of internal controls relevant to the audit in order to design audit procedures that are appropriate in the circumstances, but not for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the government's internal controls.  Evaluate the appropriateness of accounting policies used and the reasonableness of accounting estimates and related disclosures made by the management.  Obtain an understanding of internal controls relevant to the audit in order to design audit procedures that are appropriate in the circumstances, but not for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the Government's internal controls.  Conclude on the appropriateness of management’s use of the going concern basis of accounting and, based on the audit evidence obtained, whether a material uncertainty exists related to events or conditions that may cast significant doubt on the government’s ability to deliver its mandate. If I conclude that a material uncertainty exists, I am required to draw attention in my auditor's report to the related disclosures in the financial statements or, if such disclosures are inadequate, 9 to modify my opinion. My conclusions are based on the audit evidence obtained up to the date of my auditor's report. However, future events or conditions may cause the government to fail to deliver its mandate.  Evaluate the overall presentation, structure, and content of the financial statements, including the disclosures, and whether the financial statements represent the underlying transactions and events in a manner that complies with the Government of Uganda Public Financial Management laws and regulations. I communicate with the Accounting Officer regarding, among other matters, the planned scope and timing of the audit and significant audit findings, including any significant deficiencies in internal controls that I identify during my audit. I also provide the Accounting Officer with a statement that I have complied with relevant ethical requirements regarding independence and communicate to the Accounting Officer all relationships and other matters that may reasonably be thought to bear on my independence, and where applicable, actions taken to eliminate threats or safeguards applied. From the matters communicated to the Accounting Officer, I determine those matters that were of most significance in the audit of the financial statements of the current period and are therefore the key audit matters. I describe these matters in my auditor's report unless law or regulation precludes public disclosure about the matter or when, in extremely rare circumstances, I determine that a matter should not be communicated in my report because the adverse consequences of doing so would reasonably be expected to outweigh the public interest benefits of such communication. Other Reporting Responsibilities In accordance with Section 18 (1) of the National Audit Act (NAA), Cap 170, I report to you, based on my work described on the audit of Financial Statements that, except for the matters presented below and those in Section 2 of this report, whose effect has been considered in forming my opinion on the financial statements, the activities, financial transactions and information reflected in the Consolidated financial statements that have come to my notice during the audit, are in all material respects, in compliance with the authorities which govern them. 1.4 Review of Double Taxation Agreements A Double Taxation Agreement (DTA) is a bilateral agreement between two countries that aims to prevent the same income or capital from being taxed twice. This situation, known as double taxation, often arises in international trade and investment. These treaties are entered into by capital-importing countries, such as Uganda, to promote or attract investment by reducing the cost of overseas investment for capital-exporting countries. Currently, Uganda is party to nine (09) Double Taxation Agreements with several countries. I reviewed the operations regarding the treaties and made the following observation; 10 1.4.1 Lack of Key Statistics in Regard to Revenue Foregone vis-à-vis Investment Promotion Tax treaties shift taxing rights away from the capital importer (a developing country) towards the capital exporter (a developed country). The capital importer is expected to benefit from the welfare gains from increased inward investment, which is expected to outweigh the fiscal costs (revenue foregone). I noted that no centralised statistics highlighted the benefits accruing from the existing DTAs, relative to the revenue foregone by them. Reliable statistics would enable the country to evaluate the extent to which it benefits from being a party to these DTAs. Without reliable statistics on the DTAs, it becomes impractical to assess the viability of these treaties, leading to inadequate decision-making. The Accounting Officer explained that previously, URA’s income tax returns were not designed to capture key information on taxpayers benefiting from Double Taxation Agreements (DTAs). However, under the Government’s tax expenditures management framework, it was agreed that URA would amend the returns before the end of FY 2025/26 to ensure that the necessary DTA-related data is collected. The Accounting Officer further explained that once this information is in place, the Government will undertake a cost–benefit assessment starting FY 2026/2027 and identify appropriate policy reform measures. Recommendation I advised the PSST to expedite the assessment of all DTAs to determine the country’s benefit from the agreements. 1.5 Taxation of Digital Services Over the last decade, world trade has evolved, with a growing proportion of services now offered through digital channels. Some of the services include entertainment services, Advertising services and other social media, cloud computing and software subscriptions from various software providers, betting services through online betting platforms, and education services through online tuition providers, among others. These services imply that significant income flows out of the country to various non- resident service providers. The Income Tax Act was amended in FY 2023/24 to introduce a 5% Digital Service Tax for non-resident persons providing digital services to customers in Uganda. I noted that during the year 2024/25, UGX.29.583Bn was collected from the Non- Resident Digital Service providers through Income Tax and VAT. Section 86(4) of the Income Tax Act, Cap 338, requires a resident company to lodge a tax return with the Commissioner, within 15 days after the end of a tax period. I reviewed the taxation of digital services and noted the following; a) Although some non-resident digital service providers (DSPs) submitted tax returns under the Digital Service Tax (DST) regime, URA lacked a mechanism 11 to verify the accuracy or completeness of the declarations. In effect, URA is entirely reliant on self-declarations by the non-resident service providers. b) UGX.29.583Bn was collected in 2024/25 from 82 Non-Resident Digital Service Providers through Income Tax and VAT. The list, however, was not conclusive, as it missed many known providers. Lack of visibility into payments made to non-resident digital service providers limits URA’s ability to independently validate DST declarations, which exposes the Authority to Revenue leakage due to under-declaration or non-declaration of taxable income. The above also implies that some companies are generating revenue in Uganda without paying the applicable taxes. The Accounting Officer explained that the Bank of Uganda was in the process of procuring a single national payment gateway system. The Ministry was working with BOU to ensure that the procured system enables URA to have timely access to all information needed to enforce compliance among non-resident digital service providers. Recommendation I advised the PSST to continuously engage the Bank of Uganda to expedite the creation of a single national payment gateway system, to enable visibility into payments to these Digital service providers. 1.6 Review of GoU Funded Projects Over the last 15 years, the Government has focused on increasing public infrastructure investment to reduce the infrastructure gap, thereby improving private investment and the business climate and achieving socio-economic transformation. In line with the PFM regulations, the Development Committee (DC), presided over by the PS/ST, was set up to serve as the high-level technical organ responsible for performing the ‘gatekeeping’ role within the Public Investment Management System Framework. I reviewed the project performance as reported in the project master file and project budget performance data from 2020/2021 to 2024/2025 and noted that the government budgeted solely to fund 106 projects worth UGX.13.3Tn. However, only UGX.10.07Tn was released to the projects, leading to a shortfall of UGX.3.2Tn (24%). Details in the table below; Table 5: Budget Performance for projects solely funded by the GoU SN F/Y Budget (UGX Tn) Release (UGX Tn) Expenditure (UGX Tn) Funding Variance (UGX Tn) 1 2020/2021 2.8 1.65 1.60 1.20 2 2021/2022 2.2 1.99 1.93 0.24 3 2022/2023 2.8 1.97 1.97 0.80 4 2023/2024 2.7 2.32 2.26 0.43 5 2024/2025 2.7 2.12 1.74 0.59 Total 13.3 10.07 9.52 3.26 24% Source: OAG analysis 12 A further analysis of the project data revealed the following; 1.6.1 Slow Progress in Implementation of the Projects Section 5.1 of the Development Committee (DC) Guidelines requires that, in order to ensure efficient and effective implementation of public investments in the country, the DC undertakes annual portfolio reviews of all ongoing projects in the Public Investment Plan (PIP) in line with the DC calendar. I reviewed the decision matrix of the annual portfolio review as at 30th June 2025 for 106 GoU-funded projects and noted slow implementation as detailed below;  Three (03) projects were downgraded to the pipeline to await funding and re- inclusion in the PIP.  Thirty-six (36) projects were exited, out of which only five (05) had been successfully completed, twelve (12) had reached the end date, six (06) projects received various extensions to complete activities in vain, while eleven (11) projects had not registered progress as at 30th June 2025.  Seven (07) projects were extended due to numerous unsettled PAPs, re- scoping of projects, glaring implementation challenges ranging from land acquisition, cash flow constraints and delays in completion of designs, among others.  Sixty (60) Projects were retained in spite of their implementation challenges.  I noted that there was no evidence on the Integrated Bank of Projects (IBP) of evaluation of completed, exited and downgraded projects in relation to the planned outputs, outcomes and impacts in line with the established objectives in the project design. I further noted that despite the slow implementation of projects as at 30th June 2025, the Government on-boarded 149 new projects, solely funded by GoU, worth UGX.19.584Tn on 1st July 2025. It is apparent that the project portfolio's performance is below average, due to the evident implementation challenges encountered during project execution. The PS/ST explained that he had issued a framework for tracking the implementation and performance of public investments, aimed at standardising and providing strategic direction during project implementation, and that the MoFPED was in the process of upgrading the IBP to enhance its robustness and facilitate real-time project reporting on both financial and Physical performance. Recommendation I advised the PS/ST to ensure compliance with the framework to fast-track the efficient and effective implementation of projects and enable the attainment of the intended objectives. 13 1.6.2 Lack of a data bank with cumulative costs incurred on project execution and other project information Section 4.31.1 of the Treasury Instructions provides that Projects shall be monitored to assess progress relative to the implementation plan by the Implementing agencies submitting monthly and quarterly progress reports to identified monitoring agencies that shall assess financial and physical implementation. Section 7.4 of the Development Committee (DC) Guidelines states that the DC shall be supported by the IBP to enable smooth operations. The IBP is a single window system for all stakeholders involved in the Public Investment Management System of Uganda. It also serves as a central repository of information about public projects from preparation, budget formulation, execution, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation to closure. I reviewed the Integrated Bank of Projects (IBP) and the project master file and noted the absence of cumulative project costs incurred for all projects in the portfolio. I further reviewed the project performance by agreement report (for projects with an external funding component) and revealed that;  Three (3) projects (Bukasa Inland Port, Development of BTVET, and development of Kabaale International Airport) received full funding, but the master file did not indicate the cumulative funding received and spent.  Twenty-one (21) sampled Projects on the decision matrix availed could not be found on the IBP despite the requirement that all project information should be uploaded on the IBP. There is a risk that projects have received over and above the project's proposed costs/value over time due to the lack of effective monitoring of the financial implementation of the respective projects. There is also a risk that the IBP is not updated with all relevant project information as required by the Development Committee guidelines. The Accounting Officer explained that there was a planned upgrade of the IBP aimed at fully integrating it with other PFM systems to ensure that all project-related information from inception to closure is available on the IBP. Recommendation I advised the PS/ST to implement measures to ensure compliance with the Development Committee guidelines, in line with the upload of project data to the IBP. 14 1.6.3 Inconsistent Application of GFSM Frameworks in Budget Preparation and Classification The Government Finance Statistics Manual (GFSM) is a series of guidelines issued by the IMF that describe a specialized macroeconomic statistical framework (the government finance statistics (GFS) framework) to support fiscal analysis. The Public Finance Management Act, Cap 171, sets out a legal framework for economic management to ensure macroeconomic stability. Section 3(2) of the Act provides for the principles that must be based upon while setting the Government’s fiscal objectives. The updated Chart of Uganda Accounts, May 2022, indicates that the Government adopted a financial reporting framework that conforms to the 2014 IMF Government Financial Statistics (GFS), which requires Governments to align their budget classification, reporting, and fiscal analysis to strengthen the worldwide effort to improve public sector reporting and transparency. I noted that whereas Government adopted the GFSM 2014 classification structure in its Chart of Accounts for coding and reporting, budget preparation and presentation processes were undertaken using the GFSM 1986 framework, yet the GFS 2014 is superior to the GFS 1986 in some of the following aspects; Table 6: Differences in GFSMs Aspect GFSM 2014 GFSM 1986 Key Difference Basis of Recording Economic Events Records all economic flows on an accrual basis, capturing transactions when economic value is created, transformed, exchanged, or extinguished. Records transactions only when cash is received or paid (cash basis). GFSM 2014 provides a more comprehensive and timely reflection of government activities and obligations. Coverage Captures transactions of the public sector and its subsectors, on an institutional basis consistent with the 2008 System of National Accounts (SNA). Uses a functional approach, including all entities performing government functions but excluding some market activities. GFSM 2014 ensures institutional consistency, while GFSM 1986 focused on government functions. Analytic Framework Introduces multiple balancing items such as net operating balance and net lending/borrowing, allowing multidimensional fiscal analysis. Focuses on a single balancing item, the overall deficit/surplus. GFSM 2014 enables broader fiscal analysis and sustainability assessment. Balance Sheets Includes complete balance sheets covering nonfinancial and financial assets, liabilities, and net worth. Reports only stock positions of certain debt liabilities. GFSM 2014 provides a full view of the government’s financial position and net worth. Source: GMFS Framework 15 The misalignment makes it difficult to track fiscal aggregates in line with GFSM 2014 definitions. The Accounting Officer explained that the Accountant General had undertaken a progressive transition from cash to accrual accounting, including recognition of fixed assets in the statement of financial position. As a final step in this transition, the Ministry is reviewing Schedule 3 of the PFMA Cap 171, to align the classification of Budget Information with GFS 2014, effective FY 2027/28. Recommendation I advised the PS/ST to expedite efforts to harmonise the budget preparation, classification, accounting and reporting processes with the GFSM 2014 framework. 1.7 Review of UDC Capitalization State enterprise, Uganda Development Corporation (UDC) is mandated to promote and facilitate industrial and economic development by investing in commercially viable projects that align with the National Development Goals. Although UDC is expected to operate with a degree of independence, it is being financed through project-specific funding. The government releases funds to UDC that are already earmarked for specific projects, leaving UDC with no space to conduct proper investment appraisal. I noted the following; i) Over the last 10 years, UDC has invested UGX.1.3Tn in 22 companies through various modalities. Assessment of 10 active companies that provided documentation revealed that;  8 out of 10 companies recorded net losses for at least two consecutive years.  Kaaro-Koffi Ltd, despite an investment of UGX.3.1Bn, remains non- operational four years after the initial investment.  Eight companies that UDC loaned UGX.23Bn had not adhered to the agreed repayment terms and had neither paid principal nor interest.  An assessment of UDC’s investment income for the year revealed a paltry UGX.1.4Bn against a UGX.1.3Tn investment, giving a return on Investment of 0.09%. The above analysis shows that the investment decisions made for UDC are not yielding returns. The Accounting Officer explained that UDC’s Strategic Plan 2020-2030 envisaged the Corporation’s impact to be measured through achievement of high-level outcomes anchored upon five fundamental principles, namely; a) Creation of both direct and indirect employment with a focus on productive jobs. b) Utilization of local raw materials/resources to manufacture for both the domestic and international markets. 16 c) Improving the trade balance position as envisaged in the National Export Development Strategy, the National Industrial Development Policy, and the National Investment Policy, among others. d) Development of Local Entrepreneurship. e) Balanced regional development. The contribution of UDC and achievements in job creation, trade balance improvement, agro-industrial development, and regional equity over the past five financial years include: Job creation/retention, Utilization of Local Raw Materials/Resources, Improving the trade balance position, Contribution to Import Substitution, Development of Local Entrepreneurship and UDC’s Commitment to Balanced Regional Development. Government will consider financing the Fund to support national priority investments that have a high development impact but low returns, or that take too long to turn around to profitability, to free UDC capitalization for investment in entities that provide good returns on investment. Recommendation I advised the PS/ST to consider providing capital funding to UDC and then demand an expected return on investment. Edward Akol AUDITOR GENERAL KAMPALA 31st December, 2025 17 SECTION 2: REPORT ON THE AUDIT OF COMPLIANCE WITH THE RELEVANT REGULATORY FRAMEWORK I conducted compliance audits on selected key subject matters in line with Section 18 of the National Audit Act (NAA), Cap 170 and in accordance with the International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions (ISSAI 4000)1 on compliance auditing. The primary objective of the audits was to obtain sufficient and appropriate audit evidence to form a conclusion on whether the Government complied with the relevant identified criteria. The areas of focus for the compliance review were;  Management of PDM, and  Management of Procurement. Audit Criteria The criteria for the audits were based on Acts of Parliament, regulations, and manuals/guidelines that are intended to be followed during implementation of the stated interventions. I therefore designed audit procedures to assess the extent of compliance. Audit Methodology My audit was conducted based on the information and records provided by the Government staff. In executing the audits, various approaches were exercised, which included;  Document reviews;  Physical inspections;  Interviewing relevant officials of the Ministry/entity; and  Analyzing data provided. Audit Findings The material findings with respect to the compliance criteria for the applicable subject matters are as follows; 1.8 Management of the Parish Development Model The Parish Development Model (PDM) is a strategy for service delivery by the Government of Uganda to improve the incomes and welfare of all Ugandans at the household level by transforming 39% of households from a subsistence economy to a money economy, as approved by Parliament. In the financial year 2024/25, the Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development (MoFPED) released UGX.1.100Tn to 10,594 PDM SACCOs as Parish Revolving Funds (PRF) - UGX.1.059Tn and administrative costs - UGX.0.41Tn as appropriated by Parliament. 1 ISSAI 4000 - Compliance Audit Standard 18 I designed audit procedures to assess whether the PDM Programme has been implemented in accordance with the PDM policy and guidelines, with a specific focus on the financial inclusion pillar. I noted that the programme was operating well in aspects of funds disbursement, loan application and data capture, and this enabled the disbursement of UGX.1,058.37Bn to 10,594 PDM SACCOs, in a timely manner. However, a few compliance issues were noted and are enumerated below; Table 7: PDM review SN Audit observation Recommendation a) Disbursement of Parish Revolving Fund to the Households Paragraph of the Users Handbook for the Parish Revolving Fund (PRF) under PDM Pillar 3 - Financial Inclusion October 2022 stipulates that the money for each Parish under the PRF shall be disbursed directly from the consolidated fund (at Bank of Uganda) to the PDM SACCO bank account solely for on-lending to subsistence households in the parish who are members of a registered PDM Enterprise Group in that parish. I noted the following; i) Analysis of PRF disbursements revealed that cumulatively, out of UGX.3,258,937,043,557 released by the Government to 10,589 SACCOs, a sum of UGX.2,750,290,874,710 (84%) had been disbursed to households by the end of the financial year 2024/25. ii) In the financial year 2024/25, a sample of 115 LGs had disbursed UGX.547,726,642,073 (73%) out of the PRF received of UGX.752,689,215,356, leaving UGX.204,962,573,283 (27%) undisbursed. The Accounting Officers attributed the above to late release of funds by MoFPED, technical challenges with the PDMIS and Wendi systems, data inconsistencies and missing beneficiary information, limited capacity and compliance issues among SACCO leaders, and procedural bottlenecks in beneficiary verification and preparation. iii) I further noted that 62 PDM SACCOs could not account for PRF of UGX.106,291,286 that had been received and withdrawn from their account but had not been disbursed to households. The Accounting Officer attributed it to diversion of funds by beneficiaries, excitement or misuse during disbursement, weak oversight, and challenges in tracking funds at the SACCO and district levels. I advised the Accounting Officers to ensure timely release and full disbursement of PRF by improving beneficiary data management, enhancing SACCO oversight and capacity, and implementing strict monitoring 19 SN Audit observation Recommendation The failure to account for the Parish Revolving Fund (PRF) and the low rate of disbursement may undermine the achievement of the pillar objective of eradicating poverty. b) Implementation of Funded Projects Paragraph 32 (b) PDM - A LG Guide for Supporting Households & Enterprise Groups in Accessing Loans Under the PRF (Guide No.2), January 2023 states that a PRF has been established to ensure loans, of up to UGX.1 million per household, are provided to subsistence households through a special type of multi-purpose cooperative called the PDM SACCO. Each loan under the PRF shall mainly be used for purchasing capital inputs and operational expenditures e.g. seeds, fertilizers, acaricides, veterinary drugs etc. I reviewed loan files and carried out physical inspections in a sample of 108 LGs and observed the following; i) In 55 LGs, a total of 619 beneficiaries in 267 PDM SACCOs had implemented ineligible projects. ii) In 42 LGs, a total of 109 beneficiaries in 86 PDM SACCOs had non-existent projects. iii) In 52 LGs, a total of 328 beneficiary households did not procure the planned items required to implement the funded projects, thus leaving UGX.263,483,000 diverted to other uses. iv) In 34 LGs, a total of 2,336 households in 506 PDM SACCOs had received PRF multiple times. The Accounting Officers attributed this to off-season or delayed disbursement, unpredictable climate and market conditions, weak supervision and monitoring at parish and SACCO levels, limited guidance and capacity for beneficiaries, system errors in PDMIS/WENDI, and inadequate sensitization on approved business plans. I advised the Accounting Officers to design a policy on supervision and enforce compliance with approved project guidelines, while enhancing beneficiary training and monitoring. c) Lack of a mechanism to establish whether all subsistence households have received PRF within the Parish Paragraph 30 of the Circular from the PSST to Accounting Officers of Local Governments and the Executive Director of KCCA (Ref: EDP 86/103/02 Vol.4, dated 27th January 2025 indicates that in some parishes, all identified subsistence households have already received UGX.1Mn each. In such instances, the Accounting Officer must promptly report these parishes to the Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development and the Ministry of Local Government to inform policy decisions. Where it is confirmed that all eligible beneficiaries have been covered, no further disbursements shall be made until written policy guidance is provided. I advised the Accounting Officers to ensure that all pending household and PRF disbursement backlogs are promptly captured and validated in the PDMIS and FIS, and continue systematic household profiling 20 SN Audit observation Recommendation I noted that the Government lacks a comprehensive database of all subsistence households, as the registration and profiling process under the PDMIS faced numerous challenges due to incorrect identification of these households. As a result, the alternative approach to identifying subsistence households is not anchored on a specific or verifiable target of registered beneficiaries. This undermines the Government’s ability to determine when parishes have fully covered or exhausted their subsistence household populations, thereby limiting its capacity to reallocate resources effectively to other parishes. The Accounting Officers attributed this to backlogs that had not yet been entered into PDMIS and FIS due to capability challenges with ICT; however, continuous household profiling through PDMIS and SPEAR tools is underway to ensure accurate tracking and reporting. using the PDMIS. d) Preparedness for Recovery of Parish Revolving Funds Paragraph 32 of the Circular from the PSST on the implementation of financial inclusion activities under the Parish Development Model during the Stabilization Phase (Ref. No. EDP 86/103/02 Vol.3, dated 8th January 2024) states that the first PDM loans disbursed in December 2022 carried a 24-month grace period, which expired in December 2024. Accordingly, Accounting Officers are instructed to notify SACCO Boards that loan beneficiaries must commence repayment to enable the recycling of funds to other eligible members within the parish. I noted that of the beneficiaries who received PRF by December 2022, only 18,105 beneficiaries in 709 SACCOs in 30 LGs had commenced voluntary recovery, and a sum of UGX.9.34Bn had been recovered. This was attributed to;  Failure by the Accounting Officer to communicate the commencement of recovery to the SACCO Boards.  Failure to track loans disbursed outside the PDMIS.  Un-updated records in PDMIS The Accounting Officers attributed this to lack of clear guidelines from the Ministry, limited beneficiary sensitization and financial literacy, inadequate monitoring and follow-up by SACCOs and district authorities, system limitations in WENDI, and the reluctance of some beneficiaries to repay. I advised the Accounting Officers to promptly communicate recovery instructions to SACCO Boards, update all loan records in PDMIS, and intensify beneficiary sensitization and monitoring to ensure timely repayment of PRF loans. e) Failure to Close Non-Wendi SACCO Bank Accounts Paragraph 11(a), (b) & (c) of the circular from the PSST to Accounting Officers of Local Governments and the Executive Director of KCCA, Ref No. EDP 86/103/02 Vol.4 dated 27th January 2025 requires Accounting officers to ensure that; I advised the Accounting Officers to intensify follow-up with SACCO leaders 21 SN Audit observation Recommendation i) Any bank account held by a PDM SACCO for the PRF other than Government Banks should be closed; ii) Any balance on the closed account is transferred to the authorized PDM SACCO account in Government Banks. This should be done without any delay to enable the SACCOs to access the funds for lending to their members; iii) PDM SACCOs should obtain closing bank statements from the date of opening to the date of closing the account to facilitate any reconciliations, audit and other governance purposes. I noted that 5,123 SACCO bank accounts in 122 LGs, had not yet been closed, contrary to the guidance. By 30th June 2025, a balance of UGX.4,944,592,705 was outstanding on 4,974 SACCO accounts in various commercial banks. This undermines the attainment of the benefits of using the Wendi platform, which include: convenience, security, lower transaction costs, transparency and ease of tracking the PDM funds. The Accounting Officers attributed it to low response and non- compliance by banks, procedural and bureaucratic requirements, limited follow-up by SACCO leaders and district management, low account balances, and challenges in coordinating account signatories. and banks to ensure all non-WENDI accounts are promptly closed, balances transferred to authorized government accounts, and closing statements obtained for proper reconciliation and oversight. f) Inconsistencies between disbursed loans on the PDMIS platform and actual disbursements by the PDM SACCOs An analysis of centralised data from PDMIS revealed that 10,859 PDM SACCOs in 177 LGs had been cumulatively capitalised with UGX.2.9Tn, while actual capitalisation at PDM SACCOs was UGX.3.25Tn, leading to a discrepancy of UGX.294Bn. I further noted from my analysis of centralised PDMIS data that 10,859 PDM SACCOs in 177 LGs had cumulatively disbursed UGX.1.66Tn while actual disbursements at PDM SACCOs revealed that UGX.2.75Tn had been disbursed, leading to a discrepancy of UGX.1.08Tn. This was mainly attributed to loans disbursed outside PDMIS in the first year of PDM inception. I further noted that in 98 LGs, 167,819 loan records were processed outside the PDMIS. Of the records processed outside PDMIS, only 9,567 were captured in the system, leaving 158,252 (94%) uncaptured. The Accounting Officers of LGs attributed the inconsistencies between PDMIS data and actual SACCO capitalisation and disbursements mainly to the delayed update of the PDMIS with loans disbursed outside the system in the early years of PDM, arising from capacity gaps and inadequate training of local government staff, laxity in enforcing data capture, and persistent system and network challenges. I advised the Accounting Officers to, in liaison with MoFPED as the Financial Inclusion Pillar lead, the PDM Secretariat, and MoICT as custodian of PDMIS, ensure a time-bound reconciliation and mandatory capture of all loans previously disbursed outside PDMIS, supported by targeted system support, refresher training, and strengthened supervision to achieve complete and consistent PDMIS data. 22 SN Audit observation Recommendation g) Monitoring of PDM by HLGs Paragraph 7 of the Circular from the PSST to the Accounting Officer of Local Governments and the Executive Director of KCCA Ref No. EDP 86/103/02 Vol.4 dated 27th January 2025 provides that in order to facilitate national monitoring of the Programme, all Accounting Officers are required to submit a quarterly report to; Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development (MoFPED), the Ministry of Local Government (MoLG) and PDM Secretariat, not later than the 15th day after the end of each quarter. I noted that there was no evidence that 125 LGs prepared and submitted quarterly reports to; MoFPED, MoLG and PDM Secretariat. This undermines the achievement of the programme objectives. Accounting Officers attributed this to inadequate funding for monitoring and reporting, the absence of a standardised reporting format and technical guidance from the PDM Secretariat, weak internal enforcement and oversight, delayed issuance of circulars, and reliance on consolidated PBS reports instead of dedicated PDM reports. I advised the Accounting Officers to ensure that all LGs prepare and submit quarterly PDM reports to MoFPED, MoLG, and the PDM Secretariat using standardised formats and provide the necessary funding and oversight Source: OAG Analysis Conclusion The Government envisaged that the adoption of the Parish Development Model (PDM) strategy would improve service delivery and the incomes and welfare of all Ugandans at the household level by transforming 39% of households from a subsistence economy to a money economy. Whereas a lot has been done to implement the strategy, there are still notable areas that require improvement, and as such Government should consider implementing the recommendations in this report to address the challenges highlighted above for better management of the PDM. 23 1.9 Management of Procurements This section highlights my key findings, which have been consolidated for the purpose of this thematic report, details of which have been reported in the individual entity/project- specific reports. 1.9.1 Inadequacies in the standardisation of specifications and prices for common user works, services and supplies Section 8 of the PPDA Act, Cap 205, empowers the Authority, where applicable, to determine the prices of works, services and supplies which are used in common by two or more procuring and disposing entities and which may be subject to common procurement; and review the prices as may be necessary. The Authority is also mandated to adopt, adapt and update common specifications standards, the use of which shall be mandatory to all procuring and disposing entities. Audit established the following inadequacies; i) The PPDA last undertook price surveys for common user goods in 2022, and this only covered Kampala, Mbarara, Mbale, Hoima, Arua and Gulu Districts. ii) Comparison of the costs for construction of office accommodation for the ongoing and recently commissioned projects revealed variances in the costs per square ranging from UGX.5.3Mn to UGX.3.7Mn. Analysis of the costs for construction of a sample of tarmacked roads revealed variances for each square meter as detailed below; Table 8: Inadequacies in the standardisation of specifications and prices for roads SN Project Name Cost Per Square Meter (UGX/M2) 1 Upgrading to the paved standard of 8.07km and reconstruction of 6.83km roads, including signalisation of seven (7) junctions in Lubaga and Makindye divisions 609,639 2 Reconstruction of 18.84km of roads in Makindye, Central, Kawempe and Lubaga Divisions, including the Signalization of 5 Junctions in Makindye Division (Lot 3) 491,620 3 Construction of selected roads in Kira and Mukono Municipalities – Lot 1: Mbogo & Cyprian Roads (9.0km), Kungu – Bivanju road (2.3km) 299,977 4 Construction of Selected Roads in Kira and Mukono Municipalities. Lot 2: Anthony-Kame, Kame Annex, Albert Cook-Cathedral Rise, Kame-Nabuti-Katosi road, Admin Link, Access Road, Link Road (8.68Km) 357,722 5 Construction of selected roads in Kira and Mukono municipalities Lot 3: Nasuuti-Nakabago-Ntawo, Bajjo-Seeta, Serado Link, Kigunga Link (9.72km) 324,033 Source: Analysis of procurement Data 24 Analysis of the costs for furniture with the same specifications from a sample of entities also revealed wide variances, as detailed below; Table 9: Furniture costs in different entities SN Item Name Entity A Entity B Entity C Entity D (Amounts in UGX) 1 Deluxe Bullet Desk Executive Package 3,000,000 1,350,000 - - 2 Executive desk 5,000,000 4,300,000 4,915,254 7,500,000 3 Executive desk set 4,000,000 4,300,000 4,661,017 7,500,000 4 Executive high back chair 400,000 850,000 - 1,600,000 5 Executive high back chair swivel 1,000,000 1,900,000 - 1,250,000 6 Workstation 6,000,000 4,000,000 - - Source: Analysis of procurement Performance Data In light of the above, it was noticed that government was incurring different costs on common user items due to the price variances that ought to be standardized. Standardization of specifications and prices would eliminate the associated variances on costs incurred by various government entities on common user works, services, and goods and also provide a benchmark for budgeting purposes. Recommendation I advised the PS/ST and Executive Director of PPDA, in liaison with other responsible ministries and/ or subject matter experts, to undertake standardization of specifications and prices for common user works, services, and goods for all Procuring and Disposing entities to either comply or explain. 1.9.2 Non-compliance with reservation schemes Paragraph 2 of the PPDA Guideline number 11 of 2024, Guidelines to promote participation of registered associations of women, Persons with Disabilities, requires an entity to reserve at least 15% of its annual procurement plan budget for awards to registered associations of women, youth, and persons with disabilities. Contrary to the above, I noted that there was no single Ministry, Department, Agency or Local Government out of the sampled 65 entities that reserved procurements for registered associations as required by the guidelines. As such, no contract awards were made to the registered associations. The Accounting Officers attributed the occurrence to the late release of the guidelines by the Public Procurement and Disposal of Public Assets Authority. It was also indicated that provisions for special interest groups had been made in the subsequent procurement plans. 25 The failure to reserve procurements for registered associations undermines the legislator’s objective of promoting the participation of women, youth, and PWDs in public procurement proceedings. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officers to ensure that the published procurement plans indicate procurements reserved for registered associations to facilitate their participation and ensure compliance with the reservation scheme guidelines. 1.9.3 Failure to prepare multi-year procurement plans Section 60(6) of the PPDA Act, Cap.205 requires an entity that undertakes a procurement over a period of more than one financial year to prepare a multi-year procurement plan using the guidelines issued. I reviewed entities’ procurement reports for the financial year 2024/25 and noted that 64 procurements worth UGX.385Bn were initiated in prior periods and completed in the current year; however, these entities did not prepare multi-year procurement plans for the procurements as required by the Act. The failure to prepare multi-year plans creates uncertainty regarding the availability of funds, which may lead to project delays and cancellations. Recommendation I advised the Accounting officers to ensure that multi-year procurement plans are prepared for procurements expected to span more than one year for proper planning and budgeting. 1.9.4 Ambiguity in the use of lists of prequalified suppliers Regulation 53 (3) of the PPDA (Rules and Methods) Regulations, SI No. 100 of 2023, provides for an entity to develop a shortlist for bidders using the entity’s list of providers prequalified for groups of procurements which are similar, or PPDA’s register of providers, another entity’s pre-qualified list, or market knowledge. A bidder shall not be included unless they are expected to fully satisfy the qualification requirements of competence, capacity, resources, and experience required for the execution of the procurement. It was noted that the Regulations do not provide the order in which the prescribed sources of developing the shortlist of the bidders apply. Despite having a prequalified list of providers for various supplies, services and works at the entity, it was noted that some entities were shortlisting bidders other than those on their own pre-qualified lists. Failure to shortlist prequalified suppliers from the entities' own prequalified lists undermines the purpose for which the prequalification process was intended and fogs transparency. 26 Recommendation I advised the Public Procurement and Disposal of Public Assets Authority to review the PPDA (Rules and Methods) Regulations, 2023 so as to streamline the order of use of the various sources for developing shortlists of bidders. Conclusion The evidence obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for my conclusion. Based on the work performed and described in this report, except for the findings stated above, nothing has come to my attention that causes me to believe that the Management of the Parish Development Model and Procurement and disposal of Goods and Services in Government is not in compliance, in all material respects, with the relevant criteria. Edward Akol AUDITOR GENERAL KAMPALA 31st December, 2025 27 SECTION 3: REPORT ON PERFORMANCE EVALUATION In accordance with Schedule 5 of the Public Finance Management Act, Cap 171, on the presentation of financial statements, and Section 18 of the NAA, Cap 170, I undertook an evaluation of the Government’s actual performance in comparison with its planned activities and outputs for the year as well as its mandate. This section presents the findings from the evaluation of the performance. 1.10 Review of Taxation 1.10.1 Low Tax/GDP ratio According to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), developing countries should maintain a tax-to-GDP ratio of at least 15% to ensure they have the funds to invest in the future and achieve sustainable economic growth. Tax-to-GDP Ratio represents total tax revenue as a percentage of GDP and indicates the share of a Country's output that the Government collects through taxes. A comparison of the Country’s performance with other economies revealed wide disparities, as shown in the table below; Table 10: Uganda's tax/GDP performance compared to other economies Particulars Tax/GDP ratio Uganda 13.4% Recommended for Developing Countries 15% World Average 23% Sub-Saharan Africa Average 18.6% OECD Average 34% Source: UBOS and URA Data From the above analysis, it is evident that Uganda has continued to perform relatively poorly compared to other countries in the region and globally. I noted, however, that although URA efforts have yielded significant results, with tremendous growth in revenue collection, Uganda's Tax/GDP ratio has stagnated at around 13.4%. Below is an analysis of various sectors’ contribution to Tax and to GDP for the three years to 2024/25; Table 11: Uganda's various sector contributions to taxes & to GDP SN Current Sector Main Activity % Contribution to taxes FY 2023/24 % Contribution to taxes FY 2024/25 % Contributio n to GDP FY 2023/24 % Contributi on to GDP FY 2024/25 1 Agriculture, forestry and fishing 0.80 1.63 24.6 26.1 2 Mining and quarrying 1.64 2.17 1.3 1.2 3 Manufacturing 21.79 22.19 15.1 14.5 4 Wholesale and retail trade; repair of motor vehicles and motorcycles 25.76 25.46 9.4 9.6 5 Real estate activities 2.43 2.53 6.0 5.7 6 Education 1.77 1.67 3.6 3.6 28 SN Current Sector Main Activity % Contribution to taxes FY 2023/24 % Contribution to taxes FY 2024/25 % Contributio n to GDP FY 2023/24 % Contributi on to GDP FY 2024/25 7 Human health and social work activities 2.10 1.94 3.2 3.0 Source: URA The table above shows a structural imbalance between economic activity and tax revenue, with agriculture, real estate and services contributing significantly to GDP but relatively little to tax revenue. Government tax revenue remains heavily concentrated in trade and manufacturing. There is a need to broaden the tax base, enhance compliance in high-GDP but low-tax sectors, and rebalance the tax burden to better align revenue collection with the economic structure through the tax policy. The Accounting Officer explained that to enhance Uganda’s domestic revenue efforts, Government formulated a National Tax Policy, which was approved by Cabinet in FY 2024/25 and is currently under implementation. He further expounded that Government was in the process of finalising the drafting of the Domestic Revenue Mobilisation Strategy II (DRMS2), aimed at increasing Uganda’s revenue effort to at least 20% of GDP over the medium term. Recommendation I advised the PSST to expedite efforts to revise the tax policy to align with the growing GDP and revenue collection. 1.10.2 Expansion of the Tax Register The URA Financial statements for FY 2024/25 indicated an addition of 728,640 taxpayers to the register, bringing the total number of registered taxpayers to 5,251,874; however, only 20% of these are active. I noted that, whereas efforts were invested in growing the register through the TREP program, other clusters of potential taxpayers were not considered for inclusion on the register, yet they are expected to yield significant revenue, as explained below;  Practising Accountants Out of 289 accountants registered with the ICPAU, only 104 were compliant and had filed up-to-date returns; a sample of 10 were registered with URA but had either never filed returns or had returns that were not up to date. 29  Practising advocates Out of 1271 advocates registered with the Uganda Law Society, only 292 were compliant in terms of having up-to-date Income Tax Returns. 249 were registered with URA but did not have up-to-date Income Tax returns, while 61 were not traceable on the E-tax system and, therefore, most likely not registered with URA.  Similar disparities can be noted in the education, health and engineering sectors. It should be noted that Section 4(8) of the Income Tax Act, Cap 338, bars persons providing professional services, such as accountants and advocates, from filing under the presumptive tax regime. The above cases imply that there are still untapped areas that URA has not leveraged, to effectively and efficiently collect revenue. The Accounting Officer explained that Government had amended the Tax Procedures Code Act (TPCA) to require the possession of a Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) prior to licensing by any regulatory authority, as provided under Section 4(9) of the TPCA. Accounting Officer further explained that URA had been guided to update the tax register and enforce compliance to address these gaps. Recommendation I advised the PSST to institute measures to ensure that the URA enforces the requirements of the amended Tax Procedures Code Act (TPCA). 1.11 Review of Fiscal Operations 1.11.1 Revenue performance I assessed the performance of the resource envelope (resources provided to fund the expenditure budget). Details of the performance of the resource envelope are shown in the table below; Table 12: Revenue performance Revenue source Budgeted amount (UGX Tn) Amount realised (UGX Tn) Variance (UGX Tn) Tax revenue 29.37 30.46 (1.09) Non-tax revenue (Including Local revenue Government collections) 2.91 2.24 0.67 Domestic Financing 8.97 13.33 (4.36) Domestic refinancing 12.02 12.21 (0.19) Withdrawals from the petroleum fund 0.12 0.28 (0.16) External sources Budget and project support 10.97 5.20 5.77 Total 64.36 63.72 0.64 Source: URA revenue collections, BoU auction results and DMFAS 30 Overall, the total resource amounted to UGX.63.72Tn against a budget of UGX.64.36Tn, resulting in a net shortfall of UGX.0.64Tn. The gap was largely driven by the weak performance of external financing and non-tax revenue performance, which was partially offset by higher domestic borrowing. The Accounting Officer explained that externally funded projects have been underperforming due to several factors, including mismanagement of counterpart funding. Recommendation Government should identify and address bottlenecks that led to specific revenue sources performing below expectations. 1.11.2 Expenditure Performance During the FY, Parliament appropriated a total of UGX.78.708Tn across the various expenditure categories as shown in the table below; Table 13: Various expenditure categories Category Initial budget (UGX Tn) Revised budget (UGX Tn) Amount warranted (UGX Tn) Amount spent (UGX Tn) Recurrent - Wage 7.94 8.18 7.80 7.46 Recurrent - non-wage 48.68 52.42 49.07 45.66 Capital development 15.53 18.11 15.29 9.88 Total 72.14 78.71 72.054 63.00 Source: IFMS and PBS Note: the total figures are inclusive of disbursments for externally funded projects Of the total amount warranted to cater for wage expenditure, UGX.7.46Tn was spent, representing 95.67% utilization. In addition, out of the UGX.48.97Tn warranted to cater for non-wage expenditure, UGX.45.66Tn was spent, representing a utilization rate of 93.24%. In contrast, capital development registered the weakest utilization performance, with only 64.65% of the warranted budget utilized. The Accounting Officer explained that under absorption of capital budget was attributed to delayed procurement processes, Prolonged Land acquisition processes, inadequate budget provisions, limited capacity of the Contractors, and changes of designs during execution, among others. He further explained that the Ministry is currently considering a reform to centralize counterpart funding under the Office of the Accountant General and pledged to undertake further investigations, as recommended, to address the identified issues and improve capital budget absorption. 31 Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer to comprehensively investigate the underperformance in the capital expenditure and clear any bottlenecks that hinder absorption. 1.11.3 Review of the budgetary allocation by administrative heads versus readiness to implement the 10-fold growth strategy Paragraph 36 of the tenfold growth strategy, 2025, provides that the services sector, followed by agriculture and lastly industry, had the highest multiplier effects on the economy of 2.61, 2.55 and 2.30, respectively. Paragraph 39 of the Tenfold Growth Strategy 2025, provides for four anchor areas for attaining a sustainable breakthrough into a new and higher economic frontier. These four anchor areas, referenced as the ATMS, are;  Agro-Industrial Development  Tourism Development  Mineral-based Development plus Oil and Gas (petrochemical industry) and  Science, Technology, ICT and Innovation, including ICT and the Creative Industry (Knowledge Economy). Para 40 of the same strategy provides for enablers to assist the ATMS in the achievement of the tenfold growth. These enablers include infrastructure, security, human capital, law, and order. In addition, paragraphs 46, 56 and 100 of the NDP IV, provide that the NDP IV is anchored on the Tenfold strategy, which aims to achieve economic growth of USD.500Bn within the next 15 years. The strategy emphasises accelerated investment and policy prioritisation in these growth pillars to achieve a tenfold increase in GDP by 2040. In addition, the strategy emphasized enablers. I reviewed the budgetary allocation to ATMS programs for the FY 2024/25 and noted marginal allocations compared to their strategic importance under the Tenfold Growth Strategy, as shown in the chart below; 32 Figure 1: Budgetary allocation by ATMS and Other Programs Source: analysis of information from BPS and IFMS Note: The Total revised budget the FY 24/25 is UGX.78.794Tn The graph above indicates an allocation pattern that does not prioritise productive and export-led growth in ATM sectors, which are central to the Tenfold Growth Strategy’s implementation framework. However, while the current budget heavily invests in intermediate programs that form the enabling foundation, such as infrastructure, security, human capital and law and order, the investment in the ATMS is still paltry. The above implied that there was a disconnect between strategic priorities and fiscal commitments. The Accounting Officer explained that the “ATMS Accelerator Actions Tracker” was developed and completed, and that it monitors the extent of allocations to the accelerator actions in the budget. He further explained that the allocation of resources to the ATMS in FY 2025/26 has been comprehensive and will have a higher multiplier effect in the outer years of the strategy, accelerating economic growth. Recommendation I advised the PS/ST to operationalize program strategies consistent with the Tenfold Growth roadmap. 33 1.12 Audit of Public Debt 1.12.1 Public Debt Portfolio Analysis There has been a steady increase in total public debt from UGX.69.20Tn in June 2021 to UGX.115.403Tn in June 2025, representing an overall growth of approximately 66.76% in 5 years. The graph below shows the trend of public debt over the years; Graph: Public debt portfolio over the years Source: Analysis of information from DMFAS The growing preference for domestic borrowing heightens interest and refinancing risks, since domestic instruments carry higher yields and shorter maturities, increasing the cost of debt servicing and crowding out the private sector. 34 The Accounting Officer explained that Government is intentional about rebalancing its debt portfolio by increasing access to concessional external financing through various debt management interventions. Recommendation I advised the PSST to rebalance the debt portfolio towards acquisition of concessional external financing and lengthen domestic debt maturities to reduce rollover risks. 1.12.2 Analysis of External Debt a) Analysis of external debt by category of financier Uganda’s external debt as at 30th June 2025, comprised Multilateral Creditors, Bilateral Creditors, and Commercial Banks. This trend is an indicator of improved borrowing terms, hence reducing short-term refinancing risk. 1.12.3 Trend of external debt over the years Uganda’s external debt has shown an upward trend over the years, with a cumulative increase of UGX.12.387Tn from FY 2020/21 to FY 2024/25.
