Details in the table and graph below; Table 16: Growth in external debt over the years Financial year Amount (UGX Tn) Increase (UGX Tn) % Change 2024/25 56.384 1.935 3.55 2023/24 54.449 1.257 2.36 2022/23 53.191 4.763 9.84 2021/22 48.428 4.431 10.07 2020/21 43.997 - - Source: DMFAS Source: analysis of information from DMFAS The graph above illustrates an upward trend in external debt stock over the years, increasing from UGX.43.997Tn in FY 2020/21 to UGX.56.384Tn in FY 2024/25. The graph shows a consistent but slow rate of debt accumulation over the years. 36 1.12.4 Primary dealership system in the issuance of Treasury Instruments The Treasury has delegated the process of issuance of Treasury bills and bonds to Bank of Uganda. At the moment, Bank of Uganda is using the primary dealership system for the issuance of instruments. The primary dealership system limits the bidders for Treasury bonds and bills to a few institutional players. Currently, there are eight major banks acting as primary dealers in Uganda; however, of these eight, only four are quite active. The major advantage of using the primary dealership system is the reduction in refinancing risk and the existence of price discovery through the secondary market. However, the benefit of price discovery is currently not met in Uganda, as most primary dealers hold the instruments until maturity due to an underdeveloped secondary market. I performed an analysis of the performance of the private sector commercial lending rates, compared to 10-year Government Bonds, using STATA 14.0 for the last three FYs to enable an assessment of price discovery and market efficiency. STATA is an integrated statistical software package for data management, analysis, and visualisation. The analysis compared the Yield to Maturity (YTM) on 10-year Government bonds with prevailing private sector commercial lending rates over the same period to assess pricing behaviour in the domestic debt market. Descriptive statistics examined the level and volatility of bond yields relative to lending rates. The yield spread analysis assessed the margin between risk-free government borrowing and private sector credit. The results are summarised below; Table 17: Open market operations Indicator Government 10-Year Bond Commercial Lending Rate Mean Interest Rate (%) 16.07 18.20 Standard Deviation 0.82 1.03 Average Yield Spread (Lending – Bond, %) 2.24 – Minimum Spread (%) -0.60 – Source: Analysis of market information using STATA Results from the descriptive analysis The average private sector lending rate stood at 18.20% over the period, while average Government bond yields were 16.07% (10-year), leaving a narrow margin of 2.13%, despite Government securities being risk-free instruments. In addition, the volatility (standard deviation) of the 10-year bond yields (0.82) was comparable to that of the lending rate (1.03), indicating that Government bond pricing exhibited similar instability to private credit markets. More critically, spreads turned negative during the three years, reaching as low as - 0.60% (10-year), implying that Government borrowing costs, occasionally exceeded private sector lending rates. 37 The results above suggest that the low yield spreads with bond yields averaging 16.07% are an indication of weak price discovery and limited competition in the Government securities market This exposes Government to the principal risk of the primary dealership system of limitation to competition, and the corresponding potential incentive to collusive behaviour. This may have the effect of pushing interest rates on Government instruments high as the primary dealers seek to maximise profit. Management acknowledged the recommendation and planned to select Primary Dealers with a mindset to enhance competition in the subsequent selection process. Recommendation Treasury is advised to expedite the reassessment of whether the current issuance system is optimal and take appropriate steps to address any deficiency. 1.12.5 Review of sovereign credit indicators Sovereign credit ratings are a condensed assessment of a government’s ability and willingness to repay its public debt both in principal and in interest on time. In this, they are forward-looking qualitative measures of the probability of default put forward by rating agencies. I undertook an analysis of selected sovereign credit indicators used to assess a country's creditworthiness, reflecting its ability to meet its debt obligations. For this assessment, I have assessed the indicators that measure the financial strength of a country. The financial strength parameter indicates a country’s fiscal health and its ability to manage public resources efficiently. Strong financial indicators contribute to higher sovereign credit ratings and investor confidence, while weak indicators can lead to reduced creditworthiness and higher borrowing costs. a) Public Debt to GDP Ratio - Assessment of debt sustainability – 50.29% The Debt-to-GDP ratio is a measure that compares what a country owes (total debt) and what it produces (manufactures or services). A lower ratio indicates better debt sustainability, while a higher ratio suggests increased fiscal pressure and potential challenges in meeting debt obligations. Objective 1(a) of the National Charter for Fiscal Responsibility FY 2021/22 – FY2025/26 provides that the total public debt in nominal terms is reduced to 51.2% of GDP in the financial year 2024/25. A re-computed the debt-to-GDP ratio over the years revealed a generally stable ratio in the FYs 2020/21 to 2023/24. However, during the period under review, the debt-to-GDP ratio rose sharply to 50.29%. The table and graph below refer; 38 Table 18: Public debt to GDP Financial Year GDP (UGX Bn) Total debt (UGX Bn) Debt to GDP ratio 2020/21 148,310 69,202 46.66 2021/22 162,750 77,888 47.86 2022/23 183,004 85,640 46.80 2023/24 203,708 93,608 45.95 2024/25 227,875 114,604 50.29 Source: UBOS and DMFAS Graph showing the Debt to GDP ratio Source: Analysis of information from DMFAS and UBOS Whereas there was a downward trend from 2021/22 to 2023/24, the increase in the debt-to-GDP ratio in FY 2024/25 indicated that debt grew much faster than GDP, driven by a rise in total public debt by UGX.20.996Tn in the period under review. The increase in the debt-to-GDP ratio was close to the threshold of 51.2% required under the CFR and may result in public debt becoming unsustainable in the event of an economic shock. The Accounting Officer explained that the increase was mainly due to the recognition of a lump-sum payment to BoU (through government securities), the fast-tracking of investment in the oil and gas sector to ensure first oil in FY2026/2027, and other public investments. The Accounting Officer explained that government borrowing will continue to focus on high-growth, growth-enhancing sectors in line with our ten-fold growth strategy. The Government will ensure that Uganda’s debt remains within sustainable levels, as guided by the Debt Sustainability Analysis carried out annually. 39 Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer to strengthen fiscal discipline by aligning borrowing strictly with priority development needs. b) Interest payments to total Domestic revenues Ratio – Assessment of the domestic debt service burden The National Charter for Fiscal Responsibility for the period FY 2021/22 – FY2025/26 under objective 1(b) adopted the fiscal objective of reducing the domestic debt interest payments to total revenues Ratio to 12.5% over the period of this document. This benchmark shows the proportion of the domestic revenue that goes into servicing domestic interest costs. The table below shows the assessment of the benchmark over the years. I noted an increase in the interest-to-domestic revenue ratio beyond the National Charter for Fiscal Responsibility benchmark of 12.5%. The table below refers; Table 19: Interest to total revenue ratio Financial year Total domestic Revenue – UGX Tn Total Interest – UGX Tn % of Interest to revenue Benchmark 2021/22 22.10 3.917 17.72 12.5 2022/23 25.909 4.632 17.88 12.5 2023/24 27.805 5.835 20.99 12.5 2024/25 32.093 7.594 23.66 12.5 Source: DMFAS & URA This rising trend indicates faster growth in domestic interest obligations than domestic revenues, which are consuming an increasing share of fiscal resources and reducing the Government’s fiscal space for other development priorities. If borrowing patterns are not effectively managed, this might pose a risk to debt sustainability. The Accounting Officer stated that Government is aligned with the cited recommendation, as its operations are anchored in increasing domestic revenue collections and rationalizing expenditures. Recommendation I advised the PS/ST to intensify efforts to mobilize domestic revenue and rationalize expenditure to achieve the desired benchmark. c) Fiscal deficit to GDP - Assessment of fiscal discipline A fiscal deficit occurs when a government's total expenditure exceeds its total revenue, including grants, but excluding borrowing (both external and domestic). 40 This ratio measures the size of a country's fiscal deficit relative to its GDP / how well the economy is performing. The National Charter for Fiscal Responsibility for the period FY 2021/22 – FY 2025/26 under objective 2(a) provided that the overall fiscal balance, including grants should not exceed a deficit of 4.6 per cent of non-oil GDP in the financial year 2023/24. Table 20: Performance of this ratio over the years FY Fiscal Deficit (UGX Bn) GDP (UGX Bn) Fiscal deficit to GDP ratio 2021/22 11,974.25 162,750 7.36 2022/23 10,080.79 183,004 5.51 2023/24 9,487.35 203,708 4.66 2024/25 13,719.62 227,875 6.02 Source: GoU approved estimates, GFSM framework and UBOS A high deficit-to-GDP ratio indicates possible unsustainable government spending that may prompt debt accumulation, while a lower ratio suggests more disciplined fiscal management. Although the fiscal deficit to GDP ratio has shown a declining trend over the three financial years, from 7.36% in FY 2021/22 to 4.66% in FY 2023/24 and an increase to 6.02% in the period under review, there has been an overall fiscal deficit to GDP gap as compared to the target of 4.6%. The continued presence of a big fiscal deficit calls for prudent fiscal policies to maintain long-term debt sustainability and achieve the set target. The PSST acknowledged the observation. Recommendation I advised the PS/ST to intensify efforts to realize the fiscal consolidation strategy. 1.13 Management of Non-Current Assets I undertook an assessment of the effectiveness of utilization, maintenance, and management of Non-Current Assets across fifty-seven (57) sampled entities, in line with the Treasury Instructions, 2017, and the Public Finance Management Act (PFMA), Cap 171. The review focused on asset utilization and safeguards, maintenance practices, and the recording, existence and valuation of Non-Current Assets and the following summarized issues were noted; 1.13.1 Effectiveness of Utilization and Controls to safeguard Non-Current Assets During the physical verification and review of asset registers across fifty-seven (57) sampled entities, I noted underutilized and idle Non-Current Assets worth UGX.378.022Bn in forty one (41) entities, which were not contributing to intended service delivery outcomes. 41 I noted that the entities had not put in place mechanisms to detect levels of utilization, such as operational plans and utilization reports, monitoring procedures, usage logs, and downtime records. There was also limited internal audit coverage and inadequate staff training for specialized equipment. Furthermore, Non-Current Assets valued at UGX.269.939Bn, in ten (10) entities, lacked adequate security measures, including appropriate storage, surveillance, fencing on vacant land, titling and registration of properties. These deficiencies indicate misalignment between Non-Current Assets and entity mandates, heightening risks of undetected underutilization, misuse, loss, damage, inefficient service delivery, resource wastage, unmeasured outcomes, and financial risk exposure. Recommendations I advised the responsible Accounting Officers to; i) Develop utilization plans aligned to strategic objectives; ii) Establish comprehensive asset management policies incorporating monitoring procedures, performance indicators, robust security measures, and regular reporting; iii) Secure insurance coverage for susceptible assets against risks; and iv) Conduct regular assessments to identify underutilized or obsolete assets for repurposing or disposal under the PPDA Act. 1.13.2 Maintenance of Non-Current Assets I noted that twenty-eight (28) out of the fifty-seven (57) sampled entities had no maintenance plans and reports to document maintenance requirements, such as budgets, personnel involved, and schedules. There was also no system for tracking maintenance history or forecasting future needs. Physical verification further revealed non-functional equipment/assets due to lack of servicing, worth UGX.10.533Bn, and buildings valued at UGX.61.761Bn showed signs of deterioration as a result of neglected repairs and maintenance. This was attributed to the non-integration of maintenance into broader planning and budgeting processes and failure to conduct needs assessments, which results in reactive rather than preventive approaches. This leads to asset breakdowns and structural deterioration before issues are resolved. This inadequate maintenance has led to reduced asset lifespan, potential service disruptions, increased operational costs, asset breakdowns and structural deterioration. 42 Recommendation I advised the responsible Accounting Officers to develop and implement maintenance policies with schedules aligned to manufacturer or industry standards, ensure annual approval of maintenance plans and budgets, and establish systems for tracking maintenance history and costs to maximize the useful life and value of Non-Current Assets. Edward Akol AUDITOR GENERAL KAMPALA 31st December, 2025 43 SECTION 4: REVIEW OF THE CONSOLIDATED SUMMARY STATEMENT OF FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE OF PUBLIC CORPORATIONS AND STATE ENTERPRISES FOR THE YEAR ENDED 30TH JUNE 2025 In line with Sections 12 and 18 of the National Audit Act (NAA), Cap 170, and the Public Finance Management Act (PFMA), Cap 171, I am required to audit and report on Public Corporations or other bodies established by Acts of Parliament. Section 2 of the PFMA, Cap 171 defines a Public Corporation as an authority established by an Act of Parliament other than a Local Government, which receives contributions from public funds, and any public body, which in a financial year receives any income from public funds. Similarly, a State Enterprise means a body established under any Act other than the Companies Act or a Local Government Council, and a Company registered under the Companies Act in which the Government or a state enterprise has a controlling interest. I reviewed the Consolidated Summary Statement of the Financial Performance of Public Corporations and State Enterprises for the financial year ended 30th June 2025, and noted the following; 1.14 Completeness of the Consolidated Summary Statement of Financial Performance of Public Corporations and State Enterprises Section 50(1)(c) of the PFMA requires the Accountant General to prepare and submit a consolidated summary statement of financial performance for all Public Corporations and State Enterprises where Government has a controlling interest to the Minister of Finance and the Auditor General within three months after the financial year-end. This submission is preceded by the Accounting Officers of these institutions preparing and submitting their summary financial statements to the Accountant General within two months of the end of the financial year, in line with the requirements of Section 49(2) of the PFMA. Based on my review of the consolidated summary statement for Public Corporations and State Enterprises for the year ended 30th June 2025, I noted the following; i) Sixty-two (62), representing 78% public corporations and state enterprises were consolidated in the summary statement, out of the expected seventy-nine (79). The failure to obtain information on all entities makes the consolidated summary statement of financial performance of public corporations and state enterprises incomplete. The government ownership and interest in the missing entities are concealed from the public, and it impedes informed decision-making by the relevant Government Agencies. Recommendation I advised the Accountant General to develop a comprehensive database of all Public Corporations and State Enterprises to enhance completeness, accuracy and transparency of financial reporting in the public sector. 45 1.15 Review of the Process of Consolidation of the Summary Statement of Financial Performance of Public Corporations and State Enterprises Upon the Accountant General's request for submission of summary statements of financial performance from entities, the Accounting Officers of each entity submit their respective summaries, based on unaudited financial statements. The Accountant General then utilizes the initial submissions to compile the Draft Consolidated Summary Statement. My review revealed variances between the amounts reported in the entity’s audited financial statements and their corresponding figures in the consolidated summary statement prepared by the Accountant General. The variances were partly attributed to the failure by some entities to submit adjusted summary statements of financial performance post-audit to the Accountant General. In addition, the lack of reporting guidelines has hampered the consolidation process. Recommendation I advised the Accountant General to consider issuing reporting guidelines that outline the requirements for the submission of summary statements. These guidelines should specify the use of only audited and adjusted summary statements to enhance the accuracy of the consolidation information. 1.16 Financial Performance of Public Corporations and State Enterprises I noted that out of the sixty-two (62) public corporations and state enterprises, fifty-four (54) are for-profit or with a commercial orientation, while fifteen (15) operate on a not- for-profit basis. Although public corporations and state enterprises have both commercial and service delivery mandates, the for-profit entities are expected to operate efficiently, generate profits, and pay dividends to Government. Consequently, their financial performance is of interest to Government. As highlighted in my previous reports, the Government Consolidated Summary Statement on the financial performance of public corporations and state enterprises provides limited insights, focusing only on government shareholding, total income, total expenditure, dividends declared, retained earnings, and net worth of entities. However, critical performance assessment parameters (metrics), including profitability, return on assets, liquidity assessment, and debt analysis, are absent from this reporting framework. To address this gap, I undertook an independent computation of these performance ratios based on the audited financial statements of the Public Corporations and State Enterprises. 46 Profit-Oriented Public Corporations and State Enterprises I assessed fifteen (15) entities from the fifty-four (54) profit-oriented public corporations and state enterprises. It is important to note that this analysis excluded newly established entities, recently restructured entities and entities in the investment phase. These included Uganda National Mining Company (UNMC), Kilembe Mines Limited (KML), and Uganda Development Corporation (UDC), which has twenty consolidated entities. For Uganda Electricity Distribution Company Limited (UEDCL), the company had just operated for only three (3) months, having taken over from Umeme. The financial performance analysis revealed the following; a) Profitability of Enterprises In my analysis of the profitability of fifteen (15) public corporations and state enterprises, I noted that nine (9) reported profits/surpluses during the year under review. Notable among these, were Uganda National Oil Company (UNOC) Limited (UGX.359.731Bn), Mandela National Stadium (MNSL) (UGX.92.6Bn) and National Housing and Construction Company Limited (NHCCL) (UGX.79.2Bn). However, while the Uganda Electricity Generation Company Limited (UEGCL) reported a profit of UGX.25.018Bn, this was a decline from UGX.54.282Bn reported in the previous year. The decrease was primarily attributed to the underutilization of the Karuma Hydropower Plant due to low national demand. A comparison with the previous year revealed unfavourable trends for some state enterprises and corporations. For example, Uganda Broadcasting Corporation (UBC) and Uganda Property Holdings Limited (UPHL) both registered an increase in losses, and Uganda Electricity Transmission Company Limited (UETCL) transitioned from a profit- making position to loss making. These declines were caused by reduced revenue streams without a corresponding decrease in operating costs. It is calculated from Operating income or EBIT/Total revenue. It measures the extent to which an enterprise is able to pay for its operating costs while remaining profitable. A higher operating margin means that the enterprise has less financial risk. I analyzed the operating margins of twelve (12) public corporations and state enterprises, with the objective of assessing their ability to cover operating costs while maintaining profitability. I noted that only five (5) entities reported operating margins higher than 15%, indicating strong performance. These are MNSL (94.96), NHIL (52), NEC - Luwero Industries Limited (35), UEGCL (27) and NEC Uzima Limited (24.23). The entities such as NEC AGRO SMC Limited, Uganda Post Limited and UNOC reported improvements in their operating margins compared to the prior year, despite remaining below the 15% threshold. This indicates a positive trend for these companies. However, several entities faced significant declines in their operating margins, particularly UETCL decreased from 7.36% to -23%, UBC from -3% to -24%, and UPHL from 15.5% to 5.4%. The declines reflect high operational costs and revenue drop, thus raising concerns about their financial stability. Source: OAG Analysis A decreased operating margin signals potential challenges for the public corporations and state enterprises in covering their operating costs, which poses risks to their financial stability. Furthermore, low operating margins inhibit the capacity for reinvestment and expansion, potentially stagnating growth opportunities. Recommendations I advised the affected entities to implement measures aimed at improving their operating margins by; i) Strengthening financial oversight and accountability processes and instituting better management controls. ii) Conducting reviews of companies' cost structures to identify areas for savings without compromising the quality of products or services. 50 c) Return on Assets Return on Assets (ROA) is a financial metric used to evaluate how efficient the company uses its assets to generate earnings. A higher ROA indicates more efficient use of assets, reflecting strong management performance. Although companies with substantial initial investments, such as those in capital-intensive industries, tend to exhibit lower ROA due to higher asset bases and potentially lower net income margins, a ROA below 5% is generally considered inadequate. The analysis of ROA for fifteen (15) corporations and enterprises revealed that only three (3) public corporations and state enterprises, namely MNSL, UNOC and NEC Luwero Industries Limited, achieved a commendable ROA exceeding 5%. The remaining twelve (12) exhibited low performance with ROAs falling below the 5% threshold. The Table below refers; Table 24: Returns on Assets No. Entity 2024/25 2023/24 Response (%age) 1. This points to a lack of effective asset management and strategic planning, which hinders the ability to generate income. Recommendation I advised the affected public corporations and state enterprises to conduct detailed assessment of asset conditions, to identify those due for disposal, upgrading outdated equipment, and expediting projects in the development phase to boost revenue generation capacities. d) Dividend Pay-out Several public corporations and state enterprises, despite reporting significant profits, chose not to distribute any dividends to shareholders, particularly the government. These included UNOCL, MNSL, NHCCL and UEGCL, among others. These entities cited their intention to retain earnings to fund planned investments/projects as the reason for withholding dividends. A review of financial statements and the Consolidated Summary Statement of financial performance, however, revealed that two entities declared and paid out dividends. Although the New Vision Printing and Publishing Company Limited and NHIL declared dividends of UGX.3.837Bn and UGX.0.0.271Bn, they paid out UGX.1.390Mn, UGX.0.159Bn respectively. I also noted that Housing Finance Bank Ltd, which had declared dividends of UGX.32.567Bn, did not pay at all. While retaining earnings for reinvestment may be strategically beneficial for growth, it is essential to balance this with shareholder returns. Shareholders expect return on their investment, especially in profitable entities. Recommendation I advised the Accountant General to ensure that public corporations and state enterprises develop clear dividend policies that specify how profits are allocated between reinvestment in business and dividends to shareholders. This will provide clarity and establish a framework for consistent decision-making. 53 e) Liquidity Assessment Liquidity is a measure of an organization’s ability to meet its short-term financial obligations. The Current Ratio, which compares current assets to current liabilities, is a metric used for this assessment, and an ideal (desirable) ratio ranges between 1.5 and 2, indicating sufficient liquidity to cover liabilities, although acceptable current ratios vary between different industries or sectors. In this analysis of fifteen (15) public corporations and state enterprises, ten (10) entities exhibited current ratios above the ideal threshold, suggesting they are generally able to meet their short-term obligations. Of the 10, five (5) had exceptionally high current ratios (5 and above), raising concerns about the effective utilizing of current assets or short-term financing facilities. These included MNSL, NHIL, UACC, UNOC, and UPHL. Five (5) entities fell below the desirable threshold of 1.5, indicating potential difficulties in meeting financial obligations. These included Uganda Printing and Publishing Corporation (UPPC), UBC, UETCL, URC and UPL. Below the threshold, performance was mainly attributed to an increase in payables and challenges in receivables management. The Table below refers; Table 25: Liquidity Assessment No Entity 2024/ 2025 2023/ 2024 Remarks No of times 1. Source: OAG Analysis Recommendation I advised the affected public corporations and state enterprises to implement effective working capital management strategies and enhance cash flow planning for better operational performance. f) Debt Analysis The analysis of debt ratios is crucial for assessing entity financial health and ability to meet both short and long-term obligations. The gearing ratio, which measures the proportion of an entity's assets financed by debt, is an important indicator of financial leverage and risk exposure. A debt ratio exceeding 50% is generally viewed as undesirable due to increased financial risk, although this varies from industry to another. I assessed eight (8) entities, and noted that six (6) maintained a debt ratio below the 50% threshold, indicating that owner’s equity was sufficient to cover total debt. 56 These included NEC Uzima Limited, NEC AGRO SMC Limited, NEC Luwero Industries Limited, NHCCL, URC and UPL. Two enterprises, namely UEGCL and UETCL, had debt ratios above 50%, which raises concerns about their financial stability. This was mainly attributed to inadequate funding to repay outstanding loan obligations and may further hinder the ability to access future loans. The table below refers; Table 26: Debt Analysis No. Entity 2024/ 2025 2023/ 2024 Reason/Remark (%) 1 Uganda Electricity Generation Company 81.6 88.7 The Accounting Officer explained that actions were already underway in collaboration with the MoFPED to pursue debt-restructuring options. In addition, UEGCL was committed to revenue- optimisation initiatives through improved plant availability, addressing inherent operational challenges, enhancing efficiency, and capitalizing on demand-growth opportunities. 2 Uganda Electricity Transmission Company 56 55 Management responded that during the year under review, the Accountant General advised that conversion of the loans into grants was not sustainable, after considering the requirements of International Accounting Standards, the Public Finance Management Act, and the terms of the on-lending agreements. 3 NEC Uzima Limited 0 24.3 The Company did not have any external debt financing 4 NEC AGRO SMC Limited 18.7 13.6 No Management response 5 NEC Luwero Industries Limited 8.5 18.1 Most of the company’s assets are financed by other sources other than debt. 6 Uganda Post Limited 3.2 1.3 The slight increase of 1.9% was caused by the finance lease for Post Buses and this was manageable. 7 Uganda Railways Corporation 1.60 3.81 URC’s debt ratio remained low across all periods, declining to 1.60% in FY 2024/25, which reflects minimal reliance on borrowed funds 8 National Housing and Construction Company Limited 0.04 0.03 Management stated that strategic focus is on building a stable revenue base and predictable cash flows before increasing leverage, to ensure that any future debt is sustainably serviced and development-aligned. Source: OAG Analysis Recommendation I advised the entities with high debt ratios to review their debt-to-equity mix to find an appropriate balance by developing strategies for debt reduction and/or improving operational efficiency to ensure financial stability. 57 Overall Conclusion The assessment of public corporations and state enterprises has provided valuable insights into their financial performance and operational efficiency. The objective of establishing these entities was to ensure efficient and effective management of government operations while delivering services to citizens. While some public corporations and state enterprises are performing well, there is need for efforts on those that are unprofitable, because it affects return on assets, ability to pay dividends and settle obligations, when they fall due. Implementing the recommended strategies can ensure that these entities operate effectively to fulfil their mandates while delivering services that meet the expectations of the government and the citizens. By developing appropriate financial and non-financial performance assessment indicators for Public Corporations and State Enterprises, coupled with establishing a culture of continuous improvement, the government can ensure sustainable growth and value creation through public enterprises. Edward Akol AUDITOR GENERAL KAMPALA 31st December, 2025 58 SECTION 5: SUMMARY OF FINDINGS FROM OTHER AUDIT ENGAGEMENTS In accordance with the requirements of the National Audit Act, Cap 170, I carried out various other audits in various MDAs as highlighted below; 1.17 Other audit engagements Several other audit engagements were undertaken during the year, following different audit approaches of engineering, value for money, forensic, special and Information Systems audits. Separate reports have been issued for each engagement, and summaries of findings have been included in individual entity reports. 1.18 Verification of Domestic Arrears In addition to the concluded audit engagements stated above, this office is conducting a comprehensive verification of domestic arrears across all Ministries, Departments, Agencies, and Local Authorities. The objective is to determine the accurate stock of domestic arrears for the Government. Detailed procedures have been designed to ensure that the Government's position on domestic arrears is accurately reflected. The detailed findings will be published separately. Edward Akol AUDITOR GENERAL KAMPALA 31st December, 2025 59 PART II: KEY FINDINGS FROM PROGRAMME AUDITS 2.1 Key Programme Findings This section outlines the key findings in each of the Government Programmes, based on the NDP III categorisation; 2.1.1 Human Capital Development Program 2.1.1.1 Budget Sustainability for Public Health Interventions The Ministry of Health, together with Development Partners, implements several Public Health programmes which focus on maternal and child health, prevention and control of diseases such as HIV, Malaria, and TB, provision of Mental Health services, and addressing the rising burden of Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs), among others. A review of the funding arrangements for these programmes revealed that USD.312.804Mn, which was initially provided by Development Partners through budget support, will no longer be available with effect from the financial year 2025/2026, due to changes in the Development Partners' priorities. The table below refers; Table 27: Reduction in budget support to the Health Sector No Development Partner Current Support-USD- Mn Revised/expected Support-USD-Mn Variance USD-Mn 1 GAVI-Alliance 101.443 50.721 50.721 2 Global Fund 600.327 533.744 66.583 3 Uganda Covid-19 Response and Emergency Preparedness Programme (UCREPP) 195.50 0 195.50 Total 897.27* 584.465 312.804 Source: OAG review of financial statements, correspondence and interviews with management *These are figures for entire grant or programme cycles and not annual figures. The funding from GAVI was used to support the Country's immunization efforts, focusing on Vaccine procurement and distribution. Funding from the Global Fund was for TB, HIV and Malaria control programmes, while funding from UCREPP was used for strengthening the Country's systems for Public Health Emergency preparedness. These reductions in funding will affect access to essential and life-saving medicines and medical supplies, affect disease prevention and control, infrastructure projects and the Government's ability to respond to, and manage Public Health Emergencies. Recommendation I advised Government to develop a contingency plan to minimize disruptions to Public Health services delivery programmes arising from these reductions in budget support. 60 2.1.1.2 Procurement and Distribution of Essential Medicines and Health Supplies The National Medical Stores (NMS) is mandated by Section 4 (a) and (b) of the NMS Act Cap. 207 to Procure, Store & Distribute Essential Medicines and Medical Supplies (EMHS) to all Public Health Facilities in the Country. The scope of coverage for this mandate is 3,432 Health Centres at various levels across different parts of the Country. I reviewed the procurement and distribution of EMHS and noted the following; i) The budget availed to NMS for this mandate was below the assessed funding requirements by UGX.0.181Tn. A review of the National Annual Needs Analysis and Quantification of Essential Medicines and Health Supplies for public health facilities in Uganda, compiled by the Ministry of Health and NMS, revealed that UGX.1.574Tn was required for NMS to meet the Country's EMHS demands per year. However, during the year, UGX.1.393Tn was committed, implying a gap of UGX.0.181Tn representing 11% of the required resources. ii) By 30th June 2025, NMS had Non-viable/expired drugs valued at UGX.8.04Bn made up of GoU stock worth UGX.0.53Bn and stock from Development partners worth UGX.7.51Bn. This represents a 97% decrease from the value of expired drugs of UGX.316Bn (mainly Covid Vaccines) as at 30th June 2024. These expiries were mainly due to the misalignment between the Country's medicine needs and what was procured, and changes in treatment protocols by WHO after medicines have been procured. The above shortcomings in the procurement and distribution of EMHS increase the risk of stockouts at health facilities, treatment disruption and death for patients who cannot afford to procure the medicines from private pharmacies. Recommendation I advised the Government to ensure that going forward, these challenges are addressed to minimise disruptions in the delivery of EMHS. 2.1.1.3 Functionality of ICU and Theatre Equipment The Ministry of Health procured and delivered Intensive Care Unit (ICU) equipment to 15 Regional Referral Hospitals (RRHs), three (3) National Referral Hospitals and seven (7) General Hospitals in the last five years. The records reviewed showed that the equipment was worth UGX.150Bn, and it included Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning (HVAC) systems for ICU and assorted critical-care equipment for New-born Intensive Care Units (NICU) operations. I noted that although the equipment was delivered to the facilities, several hospitals could not utilise this equipment due to gaps in ICU infrastructure, staffing, power stability and inadequate oxygen support systems. From my Interviews with hospital administrators, biomedical engineers and audit inspections, I confirmed the following; 61 i) Unreliable power supply: Five (5) hospitals lacked adequate power backup systems to support the continuous operation of critical care equipment. ICU units, oxygen plants and diagnostic machines require stable, uninterrupted electricity, yet many hospitals did not have generators with sufficient capacity, had faulty switching systems or lacked alternative power sources entirely. This challenge was observed at Hoima RRH, Jinja RRH, Mubende RRH, Fort Portal RRH and Kabale RRH. This affected the installation of ventilators, patient monitors and other ICU equipment, which remained boxed or stored in temporary rooms instead of being installed and commissioned. ii) Non-functional diagnostic equipment: Several key pieces of diagnostic equipment essential to ICU case management were either non-functional or overdue for servicing. The X-ray machines at Entebbe RRH, Hoima RRH, and Jinja RRH were non-functional due to delayed maintenance and mechanical/technical faults. The non-functional or inadequately maintained diagnostic equipment undermines the effective operation of ICU services and limits the ability of referral hospitals to provide timely and accurate diagnosis for critically ill patients. iii) Inadequate oxygen supply systems: There were gaps in the functionality, reliability and safety of oxygen supply systems. Several facilities lacked fully installed pipeline systems, had oxygen plants that were not operational, or had unresolved technical failures affecting production capacity. These challenges were observed at Mubende RRH, Fort Portal RRH, and Kabale RRH. These gaps severely limited the hospitals' ability to meet oxygen demand, particularly in ICUs, theatres and emergency units where continuous oxygen supply is essential to patient survival. iv) Inadequate maintenance budget: The health facilities were grappling with challenges of maintenance of the medical equipment due to the inadequate budget. For example, oxygen plants require quarterly servicing, yet only nine (9) of the 26 oxygen plants were serviced and only once during the year due to limited funding. In addition, the funds provided for maintenance of X-ray machines could only cover 21 of the 59 machines stationed in the various RRHs. The budget for maintenance of this equipment has remained the same at approximately UGX.7.6Bn since FY 2015/2016, despite the acquisition of sophisticated medical equipment for the Regional Referral Hospitals. This is 23% of the required budget of UGX.33Bn. These challenges collectively affected the capacity of these hospitals to deliver critical health care services despite the significant government investment. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer of the Ministry of Health and the Accounting Officers of the sampled Hospitals to address these gaps so that citizens can receive the services for which the Government made investments in the procurement of this critical ICU equipment. 62 2.1.1.4 Staffing Gaps in Critical Care Units Critical Care units refer to specialised units that provide intensive care to patients with life-threatening conditions such as severe injuries or illnesses. These include Intensive Care Units (ICUs), High Dependency Units (HDUs), Coronary Care Units (CCUs), Neonatal ICUs, Paediatric ICUs, among others. These units require highly specialised technology and trained personnel due to the criticality of the cases they handle. I reviewed the level of staffing in the critical care units of 16 Regional Referral Hospitals (RRHs) and five (5) National Referral Hospitals (NRHs) and noted acute staffing shortages. For all the staff categories, the understaffing was more than 90% and in some cases 100% as summarised below; Table 28: Staffing gaps in Critical Care Units in Regional and National Referral Hospitals No Cadre Total Approved Positions Filled Vacant % Vacancy 1. Senior Consultant (Intensivist) 20 1 19 95% 2. Consultant (Intensivist) 24 1 23 96% 3. Medical Officer Special Grade (Intensivist) 43 1 42 98% 4. Medical Officers (Critical Care) 60 2 58 97% 5. Principal Nursing Officers (Critical Care) 17 0 17 100% 6. Senior Nursing Officers (Critical Care) 68 3 65 96% 7. Nursing Officers (Critical Care) 302 28 274 91% 8. Assistant Nursing Officers 335 28 307 92% 9. Respiratory / Biomedical Technicians 12 1 11 92% Source: OAG analysis of Facility staffing records and establishments (2025) and physical inspections These staffing gaps undermine the Country's ability to provide high-quality critical care services, increase avoidable mortality, and increase the costs of treatment when a patient has to seek alternative treatment from private facilities. Recommendation I advised the MoH to work with the Ministry of Public Service and the Health Service Commission to develop a strategy to address these acute staffing gaps. 2.1.1.5 Failure to Attract Particular Health Specialists Objective 4 of the Human Resources for Health Strategic Plan (2020–2030) requires the Ministry of Health to ensure the availability of an adequate and appropriately skilled health workforce, including specialists and super-specialists who are essential for quality service delivery at all levels of care. 63 I observed that Public Health facilities are grappling with the challenge of lack of health care specialists, such as Consultant Ophthalmologists, Consultant Pathologists, Consultant Psychiatrists, and Medical Officer Special Grade in Anaesthesia and Emergency cases. These consultants typically diagnose and treat complex conditions, perform specialised medical procedures, and conduct specialised types of medical research. I reviewed the staffing requirements for selected specialists across Public Health Facilities and compared them with the actual numbers in post and noted significant variances as summarised in the table below; Table 29: Staffing levels for selected Health Care Specialists in Public Health Facilities No Post Approved Filled Vacant % vacant 1 Anesthetists 140 48 92 65 2 Psychiatrists 114 39 75 66 3 Emergency Medicine Specialists 97 33 64 69 4 Ophthalmologists 124 42 82 66 5 Pathologists 62 21 41 66 6 ENT Specialists 89 30 59 66 Source: Ministry of Health The failure to attract specialists in Public Health facilities was caused by the high entry requirements for most of these positions, which is usually a master's degree in a clinical speciality and a minimum of three years' post-qualification experience. In addition, the wage allocations to the Public Health facilities is inadequate to remunerate these specialists compared to what they are paid under private practice. The inability to attract specialists in Public Health facilities continues to undermine service delivery in critical clinical areas. This results in delayed medical care, increased referrals to private health care providers, increased risk of mortality, and forces patients to seek costly private or overseas treatment. Recommendation I advised the Government to develop a strategy and targeted interventions to attract specialists to Public Health facilities. 2.1.1.6 Management of Routine Immunisation Vaccines The Ministry of Health, through the Uganda National Expanded Program on Immunisation (UNEPI), together with the National Medical Stores (NMS), manages the procurement and distribution of vaccines to health facilities. During the year, a total of 159,902 doses of vaccines worth UGX.30.896Bn were procured and distributed to various health facilities. I reviewed the management of these activities and observed the following; i) Whereas the national cold chain infrastructure system in Public Health Facilities is largely still functional, this infrastructure is fast ageing with no clear plan of 64 replacement. Almost 50% of the current cold chain equipment was delivered over seven years ago, with low and inconsistent preventive maintenance over the past seven years. There is a risk that if this infrastructure is not replaced, the Health Facilities will not be able to keep vaccines at the required temperatures, vaccine efficacy may be affected and disruptions in vaccine access will be experienced. ii) Ten (10) districts received 1,739,119 doses of Vaccines worth UGX.17.51Bn without undertaking comprehensive needs assessments. The management of these districts explained that the estimations are usually done by UNEPI and NMS, and the districts have very limited input. This practice increases the risk of supply of vaccines that are not needed, overstocking and waste of vaccines through expiries. iii) Three (3) districts that received 266,708 doses experienced delays averaging 1- 14 days to receive vaccines. The noted delays were mainly attributed to logistical challenges faced by the NMS. These delays increase the risk of Vaccine stockouts at the health centres, leading to interruptions in the immunization programmes. iv) Twenty-seven (27) districts that received 1,761,507 doses of vaccines worth UGX.16.62Bn lacked adequate and appropriate storage facilities for the vaccines. The storage spaces were characterised by inadequate pallets, inadequate storage space, and a lack of separate storage for expired vaccines, among others. The inadequate storage increases the risk of damage to the vaccines and the associated financial loss. The above shortfalls affect the effectiveness of the vaccine distribution programme and utilisation and affect the achievement of the Government's vaccination objectives. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer of the Ministry of Health to prioritise routine maintenance and replacement of worn-out cold chain equipment in the subsequent Ministry budgets and work plans. I also advised NMS to ensure that vaccines are delivered in a timelier manner. Further, the Accounting Officers of the districts should ensure that vaccine orders are informed by proper needs assessments and that district stores are appropriate for the storage of delivered medicines. 2.1.1.7 Operationalization of the Uganda National Institute for Teacher Education The National Teacher Policy 2019, Education Sector Strategic Plan, and competency- based curriculum agenda aim to improve quality, equity, and relevance of secondary education in Uganda, with Uganda National Institute for Teacher Education established in July 2024 mandated to coordinate pre-service, in-service, and continuous professional development of teachers across six campuses of Shimoni Main, Kaliro, Kabale, Muni, Mubende, and Unyama, while Section 3.2 of the National Teacher Policy 2019 requires restructuring of teacher education under the Uganda National Institute for Teacher 65 Education (UNITE) and repurposing of 22 non-core Primary Teachers' Colleges into Technical Vocational Education and Training (TVET) institutions, health training colleges, seed secondary schools, or university campuses. However, UNITE's operationalization is constrained by inadequate funding. whereas the approved costed staffing establishment was UGX.81.1Bn , only UGX.9.1Bn (11%) was availed, leaving funding gap of UGX.72Bn (89%) resulting in recruitment of only 104 (9%) staff out of the planned 1,108, as detailed in the table below; Table 30: Staff establishment at UNITE as at 30th June, 2025 SN Position Establishment Filled Vacant %age filled 1 Academic Staff 561 43 518 8 2 Administrative Staff 320 40 280 13 3 Support Staff 227 21 206 9 Total 1,108 104 1,004 9 Source: OAG analysis of UNITE staffing data The underfunding undermines quality of teacher preparation and threatens achievement of National Teacher Policy objectives. Recommendation I advised the Ministry of Education and Sports to work in collaboration with Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development to prioritize UNITE's wage and instructional funding while interim support is provided through ministry-funded instructional material supplies. 2.1.1.8 Delayed repurposing of Non-Core Primary Teachers’ Colleges Following the approval of the National Teacher Policy in 2019, the Ministry of Education and Sports embarked on implementation of a number of reforms among which was the transition of the Primary Teacher Colleges (PTCs) from certificate to Diploma and eventually to Degree awarding institutions. This was due to the recommendation by the National Teacher Policy to have a Bachelor’s Degree as the minimum qualification for teachers at all levels of the Education system by 2031. A resolution was passed by Ministry of Education on 21st February 2023 to rationalize and repurpose the 46 PTCs. Of the 46, 23 core PTCs were maintained as Teacher Training Institutions, while the remaining 23 non-core PTCs were repurposed for other educational functions. Shimoni Core PTC was then repurposed into the main campus for the National Institute for Teacher Education (UNITE). Of the 23 non-core Primary Teachers' Colleges earmarked for repurposing, only four (18%) being Erepi PTC, Paidha PTC, Kabwangasi PTC, and Rukungiri PTC were fully repurposed and operationalized leaving eighteen (82%) institutions idle or under-utilized since 2023. 66 Continued under-utilization of these assets results in avoidable maintenance and security costs, delays expansion of secondary, TVET, and health education, and exposes infrastructure to deterioration. The delay was attributed to; inadequacies in inter-agency coordination, lack of costed implementation plan, funding constraints, and slow legal and administrative processes. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer to develop a funded time-bound repurposing plan with clearly defined roles, milestones, and monitoring mechanisms to optimize the use of existing educational infrastructure and actualise the educational reform in line with the National Teacher Policy. 2.1.1.9 Construction of Stadia and training facilities in Preparation for CHAN and AFCON games Under the East Africa PAMOJA Bid for Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) and African Nations Championship (CHAN) games, the Government of Uganda through the National Council of Sports was expected to put in place necessary infrastructure including; one stadium with 45,000 sitting capacity, two stadia with 30,000 sitting capacity each, and at least five fully functional training grounds, among others. In preparation for the tournaments, the government released UGX.941.22Bn for the construction of two stadia and one training facility. Review of the 2024 CHAN post event report by CAF and physical inspections of the facilities,revealed the following status; i) Hoima City Stadium was completed ahead of schedule. ii) VIP lounges on first floor of Mandela National Stadium were experiencing lack of air conditioning due to under designed AC system failing to accommodate increased thermal load caused by large crowds. iii) Drainage systems at Mandela National Stadium (MNS), Kyambogo University, and annexes of MNS were found insufficient to evacuate rainwater efficiently. iv) Annexes of Mandela National Stadium were facing persistent shortages in essential training equipment throughout CHAN 2024, such as; Cones and barriers for tactical drills and spatial coordination, Small goalposts for precision exercises and goalkeeper training, Rhythmic ladders to support agility and footwork routines, Refrigeration units (fridges) for hydration and medical cooling needs, Tactical boards for coaching instructions and match preparation, and Massage tables critical for recovery and physiotherapy sessions, among others. v) Maintenance conditions at Mutesa II field being below acceptable standards lacking formal pitch maintenance team and appropriate equipment. 67 vi) The construction of Akii-bua stadium and renovations to elevate Mandela stadium to CAF/FIFA standards were still expected to be completed by December 2025. vii) Mandela National Stadium Annex and Kyambogo University Training Grounds was still work in progress, with no clear completion dates. viii) The contract for renovation of Mandela National stadium had not yet been signed. The delays were attributed to slow procurement processes and limited funding. The Accounting officer explained that with the completion of Hoima Stadium ahead of schedule, Akii-bua Stadium was on course to be completed by August 2026 while the contract for renovation of Mandela phase two was in the final stages of being concluded. Recommendation I advised management of National Council of Sports to actively seek funding to complete the remaining facilities on schedule, enhance project supervision and to coordinate closely with CAF as these will ensure compliance and readiness for the AFCON games. 2.1.2 Integrated Transport Infrastructure and Services Program 2.1.2.1 Outstanding Arrears to Contractors During the year under review, I undertook a review of the outstanding arrears to contractors for the on-going road projects implemented under the Ministry of Works and Transport and the former Uganda National Roads Authority (UNRA). Based on my verification procedures I noted that as of 30th June 2025, the total outstanding arrears for unpaid completed works on road projects stood at UGX.500.347Bn. Included in this balance is UGX.73.991Bn that relates to interest on delayed settlement of outstanding certificates. The existence of the outstanding arrears was attributed to inadequate budget provisions and non-release of funds for settlement for certified works. The failure to settle these arrears exposes government to avoidable costs in the form of penalties/interest on delayed payments and the risk of litigation. In addition, delayed settlement of arrears leads to suspension of road works by the contractors which leads to deterioration of already completed works. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer to engage the PSST to prioritise settlement of these obligations. 68 2.1.2.2 Delays of Works on Road Projects I reviewed a sample of 67 road projects with a total contract value of UGX.10.625Tn, USD.400,043,710 and JPY 5,519,324,131 to assess the progress of works against the work programme. The following was observed; i) 28 projects worth UGX.3.554Tn experienced significant delays ranging from six months to over three (3) years. ii) 13 road projects had been abandoned, or works had been suspended by the contractors and at the time of writing my reports. Examples of these roads include; Mityana – Mubende- Kyejojo road, Masindi-Biiso-Kabaale-Kiziranfumbi and Hohwa-Nyairongo-Kyarushesha-Butole, road, Busega - Mpigi Expressway, Najjanakumbi – Busabala Road, Munyonyo Spur Interchange and Service roads, Ntungamo-Kabale-Katuna Road, Olwiyo – Pakwach road among others. The delays were mainly due to the lack of capacity by the contractors, delayed payments for completed works which affected the cash flows of the contractors, delays in granting the Right-of-Way, and delayed compensation of Project Affected Persons (PAPs). The delays had resulted in government paying at least USD.17,695,527.17 in commitment charges since the delays in works also affect uptake of loans by government. The delays of works also resulted in traffic inconveniences, loss of project time, and increased project costs. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer Ministry of Works and Transport (MoWT) to strengthen coordination with all responsible stakeholders especially the Parliament and MoFPED, to appropriate and provide adequate funds for the road projects. 2.1.2.3 Compensation of Project Affected Persons for Government Projects I reviewed the status of land compensations for selected government projects and noted that there were delays in compensation of PAPs which delayed acquisition of Right of Way. The cases where this was noted are summarized below. i) A total of 19,082 PAPs valued at UGX.848.46Bn were assessed for four (4) construction projects namely Bukasa Port, SGR project, Tororo- Gulu Metre Gauge and Gulu Logistics Hub project. As at 30th June 2025, 11,315 (59%) PAPs valued at UGX.315.227Bn had been paid off leaving a balance of 7,767 (41%) PAPs worth UGX.533.23Bn as unpaid. ii) I also observed that 37,595 PAPs were assessed at a value of UGX.1,163Bn for seven (7) donor funded projects. As at 30th June 2025, a total 30,998 (82%) PAPs valued at UGX.842.446Bn had been paid. The balance of 6,597 (18%) PAPs valued at UGX.320.139Bn had not been compensated. 69 iii) In addition to delayed compensation of PAPs, I also noted that out of 1,908.9 acres acquired for the SGR project, a total of 506.9 acres remained without titles. iv) I further observed that 8,263 land titles were secured from PAPs for projects implemented under the former UNRA. Out of these, 4,055 (49%) titles were yet to be subdivided to acquire the land titles and returned to the owners (PAPs). The delay in compensation of PAPs was attributed to the inadequate budgets while the delay in titling of acquired land was mainly due to lengthy and bureaucratic land expropriation and titling processes involving multiple MDAs. Consequently, the projects are exposed to encroachment and land disputes, re- occupation of the land by already compensated PAPs, escalating compensation costs, delays in implementation, and possible financial loss to Government. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer of MoWT to engage MoFPED to ensure timely release of compensation funds. I further advised the Accounting Officer to strengthen coordination with all responsible MDAs to fast-track land titling, evacuate re-occupying PAPs, and promptly return remaining titles to rightful owners. 2.1.2.4 Accumulation of Government Debtors owed to Uganda Civil Aviation Authority As at 30th June 2025, Government entities owed the Uganda Civil Aviation Authority (UCAA) a total of UGX.152.538Bn, representing 77% of the total trade debtors and receivables. These funds related to unpaid for services, security, navigation services and rent. The accumulation of long-outstanding Government debtors constrains UCAA’s cash flows and exposes the Authority to a heightened risk of revenue loss and impaired service delivery. I advised the Accounting Officer of UCAA to strengthen follow-up measures on Government debtors through inter-agency coordination with the supervising Ministries and MoFPED to ensure timely recovery of outstanding Government debts. 2.1.2.5 Road Maintenance Grant Government allocated a Road Maintenance Development Grant of UGX.1Bn to each of the 176 Local Governments (LGs), which included; 135 districts, 10 cities, and 31 Municipal Councils, resulting into a total of UGX.176Bn being transferred to LGs in the FY 2024/25. The grant is specifically designed to support road maintenance within these LGs. During my audit of the FY 2024/25, I designed audit procedures to assess the grant implementation in LGs, and below are my summary findings; 70 2.1.2.6 Road Inventory and Condition Surveys In accordance with Section 2.1 of the MoWT Road Maintenance Grant Implementation Guidelines FY 2024/25, all entities are required to prepare and maintain road inventory and condition surveys along with cost estimates. These reports must include, but are not limited to, the following information; i) Size and extent of road asset ii) Locations of culverts, bridges, drifts, road furniture and other key assets on the road network. iii) Size or scope of infrastructure to be maintained. iv) Functional hierarchy of roads. v) Volume of traffic. I noted that out of 148 LGs, 5 LGs did not have road inventory and condition surveys along with cost estimates that detailed the required information. However, 22 LGs had databases of roads which described; the size and extent of road assets, but did not have the locations of culverts, bridges, drifts, road furniture and other key assets on the road network, size or scope of infrastructure to be maintained, functional hierarchy of roads, and volume of traffic required by the roads inventory and surveys report. The absence of detailed road inventory and condition survey data hindered the efficient allocation of resources, accurate cost estimation, and appropriate prioritization of road maintenance activities. The Accounting Officers attributed this to limited funding, lack of assessment tools such as GPS devices and inadequate staff capacity. Recommendation The Accounting Officers of the LGs should liaise with MoWT and MoFPED to provide technical and financial support to develop comprehensive road inventory and condition surveys. 2.1.2.7 Status of LG Road Equipment Review of the LGs’ status of road equipment in 148 LGs revealed that; i) A total of 19 LGs did not have road equipment units. ii) A total of 137 LGs had inadequate road equipment units; these included critical road equipment such as excavators, motor graders, vibro rollers, dump trucks, bulldozers, chain loaders and wheel loaders among others. iii) A total of 119 LGs had non-functional equipment to undertake road works during the financial year. Limited availability of the road equipment delays implementation of road works, thus affects service delivery. 71 The Accounting Officers attributed this to insufficient funding of the operations of the road equipment units, as well as delays in securing additional machinery from the Ministry of Works and Transport (MoWT). Recommendation The Accounting Officers of LGs should liaise with MoFPED to secure funding for additional machinery to ensure effective and sustainable road maintenance operations. 2.1.2.8 Inspection of Implemented Road Maintenance Works Field inspection of the implemented road maintenance works in 148 LGs carried out in the period between October and December 2025 revealed that; i) A total of 239 roads measuring 1,275 kms in 66 LGs were incomplete at the time of audit inspections. ii) A total of 76 LGs had 228 roads with unsatisfactory works, such as; broken culverts, poor drainage, and uneven carriage ways with water ponding among others. This affected timely service delivery. The Accounting officers explained that maintenance of road works were affected by limited funding for road maintenance works, heavy rains, inadequate road construction equipment and un-regulated carriage load control on the LG roads. Recommendations i) The Accounting Officers of the LGs should liaise with MoWT and MoFPED to provide technical and financial support to develop comprehensive road inventory and condition surveys. ii) The Accounting Officers of LGs should liaise with MoFPED to secure funding for additional machinery to ensure effective and sustainable road maintenance operations. iii) The Accounting Officers of the LGs should ensure district engineers complete all unfinished road works, and all defects on roads should be rectified. iv) The Ministry of Works and Transport should develop comprehensive guidelines on the carriage load control on the LG roads. 2.1.3 Mineral Development Programme 2.1.3.1 Unlicensed Mineral Dealers According to section 140(1) of the Mining and Minerals Act, Cap 159, a person shall not buy or sell, as either principal or agent, any minerals or tailings unless he or she is a licensed mineral dealer. This is meant to ensure accountability and traceability of mineral transactions, which helps prevent illegal mining, theft, and smuggling. It also 72 enables the government to collect the correct taxes, royalties, and fees and reduce revenue loss. A review of the Non-Tax Revenue (NTR) schedule from URA and the Mining Cadaster Register revealed that seventeen (17) traders engaged in the buying and selling of minerals without mineral rights or a valid mineral dealer’s license. Unlicensed mineral operations led to loss of government revenue, undermined regulatory control over mineral transactions, and increased the risk of illegal mining and mineral smuggling. Management explained that, in liaison with Police Mineral Protection Unit, the Ministry has so far closed over 30 outlets of illegal mineral dealers in Kampala and will continue to follow and close up those illegal dealers operations. The Ministry will continue to undertake sensitization of URA officials in mineral related businesses and is advanced stages of joining the URA single window system where all parties can access Mineral transactions. In addition, the Ministry is establishing mineral markets and buying centers to formalize and regulate mineral trade in the country. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer to enhance monitoring of mining and mineral operations and ensure timely collaboration with URA to detect unlicensed mineral trading thus improving regulatory oversight. 2.1.3.2 Non-Functionality of Beneficiation Centers Beneficiation centers facilitate the processing of raw minerals locally and enable communities access processing equipment for better mineral recovery allowing them to earn more from value-added products rather than exporting low-value raw ores. I noted that the ministry constructed two beneficiation centers in Ntungamo and Fort portal in 2023. However, the essential beneficiation equipment had not been procured and installed. As a result, the centers remain non-functional and cannot support mineral value- addition initiatives as intended. Management indicated that the recruitment process of staff for Beneficiation centers has been completed, however, the procurement process for the Equipment was completed and delivery and installation is expected in March 2026. The Ministry is committed to the operationalization of the beneficiation centers. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer to fast track the installation of the beneficiation equipment to enable the achievement of the intended service delivery. 73 2.1.3.3 Limited Guidance on Mineral Value Addition Section 3 of the Mining and Minerals Act, Cap 159, outlines the purpose of the Act, which includes promoting and facilitating mineral trade, marketing systems, and the utilization of mineral products, as well as guiding public private partnerships in mining, value addition, and marketing. Further, Sections 127(b) and 130(b) require mineral commodities to be exported or imported only at purity levels prescribed by regulations. These provisions promote structured and transparent mineral trade, encourage domestic value addition through prescribed export purity levels, enhance revenue mobilization, attract private investments and support industrial growth ensuring that the country derives maximum economic benefit from its mineral resources. I established that although regulations prescribing purity levels exist for gold, sponge iron, and vermiculite, the majority of mineral commodities lack guidance on the allowable purity levels required before export. Further, the Ministry has not conducted comprehensive assessments to determine the extent to which each mineral can be beneficiated or value-added domestically. Notably, critical minerals such as; tungsten and tantalum lack regulatory purity thresholds, yet URA export data shows that these minerals were exported in the period under review. This indicates ongoing mining activities in the absence of clear value- addition requirements. The absence of clear guidance on mineral value-addition limits the Ministry’s ability to enforce value-addition provisions, allows continued export of minimally processed minerals, promotes illegal trading, reduces potential government revenue, and undermines opportunities for domestic industrial development in the mining sector. Management explained that the Ministry through the programme has launched a consultant to conduct a study on Mineral Value Chain Analysis (MVCA) starting with at least five critical minerals. This study will provide a comprehensive assessment to determine the extent to which each mineral commodity can be beneficiated in-country, which will enhance government’s policy direction on mineral value-addition requirements. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer to ensure timely completion of the Mineral Value Chain Analysis (MVCA) study and operationalize its findings by issuing mineral specific beneficiation requirements and putting in place mechanisms to monitor compliance. 2.1.3.4 Outstanding Mineral Sharing Deposits Section 180 (4) the Mining and Minerals Act, Cap 159, states that royalties shall be shared by the Government, Local Governments, sub county or Town Council and owners or lawful occupiers of land subject to mineral rights in a ratio of 70%, 15%, 10% and 5%, respectively. 74 I noted that the Ministry received UGX.5.862Bn into the Mineral Royalties sharing fund account in addition to the opening balance of UGX.3.913Bn from the previous period. However, UGX.8.33Bn (85%) was paid out leaving an outstanding balance of UGX.1.443Bn. Under remittance of the mineral deposits due to the beneficiaries undermines the intention of fair distribution of economic benefits arising from mining activities among stakeholders and poses the risk of conflict over resource utilization. Management explained that whereas the Ministry resolved and disbursed payments that were due to Kamwenge and Kitagwenda districts. The outstanding deposits for the two district local governments is being processed for disbursement while those due to unknown beneficiaries will be disbursed after establishment of the true beneficiaries. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer to identify bottlenecks leading to non-payment, and have them resolved on a case-by-case basis to enable payment of the outstanding royalties to the intended beneficiaries. 2.1.3.5 Non-payment of Mineral royalties Section 187(1) of the Minerals Act, Cap. 159 provides that assessed mineral royalties shall be due and payable within thirty (30) days from the date of assessment. A review of mineral royalty records in the Mine Cadaster revealed that payment of assessed royalties was not made within the prescribed thirty-day period. Consequently, royalty revenues amounting to UGX.2.82Bn remained outstanding beyond the statutory timeline. The delay in remitting mineral royalties denies Government timely revenue required to support service delivery. Failure to pay mineral royalties within the statutory 30-day period leads to delayed collection of government revenue, undermines budget execution and indicates ineffective enforcement of statutory obligations. Management explained that the Ministry, routinely serve notices of Non-compliance to any breach of the Mining and Minerals Act, Cap 159, which explicitly require the concerned licensees to settle all outstanding amounts, which include any payments for overdue royalties. The Ministry will continue to engage Attorney General’s Office and other agencies such as URA to collect the outstanding revenue. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer to strengthen enforcement of the 30-day royalty payment requirement by issuing timely reminders, applying penalties for late payment, and closely monitoring compliance through the Cadaster system. 75 2.1.4 Sustainable Development of Petroleum Resources 2.1.4.1 Progress in Oil development activities Section 10(1) of the Petroleum (Exploration, Development and Production) Act, Cap 161, indicates that one of the roles of the PAU is to monitor and regulate exploration, development and Production of petroleum in Uganda. The Government current target of first oil is mid-2026 and there are various key milestones necessary for the realization of this aspiration which include; readiness of Kingfisher development field, Tilenga development field and East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP). Government has undertaken various measures to support the achievement of these milestones. A review of the Authority’s monitoring reports for June 2025 revealed that the overall completion rates for the projects was 57.0% for Tilenga against target of 73.18%, 69.62% for Kingfisher against target of 73.18% and 62.5% for the East African Crude Oil Pipeline against planned target of 72.0%. I further noted, the National Oil Spill Response and Monitoring Infrastructure Project aimed at strengthening Uganda’s preparedness and response capacity to oil spill emergencies has not progressed due to inadequate funding. Out of the project estimated cost of UGX.59.90Bn, only UGX.1.20Bn was released over the project period of FY2022/23 to FY2024/25. Failure to achieve established project milestones and critical path deliverables poses significant schedule risks to the 2026 First Oil target and the absence of a functional emergency response capability poses unmitigated environmental and safety risks ahead of First Oil. Management indicated that measures such as pre-commissioning tests , increased work shift and establishment of an Inter-ministerial committee ,have been put in place to fast track the project implementation. As of November 2025 the status of the progress has improved and by November 2025, overall completion rates for the projects were 60% for Tilenga, 74% for Kingfisher (all wells necessary for first oil have been drilled) and 75% for the East African Crude Oil Pipeline. The Accounting Officer explained that the Authority will continue to engage MEMD and MoFPED on the issue of funding for the National Oil Spill response and monitoring infrastructure project-1780. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer to strengthen coordination with MEMD, MoFPED, and project licensees to closely monitor and fast-track delivery of critical path milestones for Tilenga, Kingfisher, and EACOP to safeguard the First Oil target, and to urgently secure adequate funding and implementation timelines for the National Oil Spill Response and Monitoring Infrastructure to ensure operational readiness and mitigate environmental and safety risks ahead of First Oil. 76 2.1.4.2 Inadequate In country product handling and storage Infrastructure Objective 3 of the Petroleum Supplies Act, Cap 163, mandates that the Uganda National Oil Company Limited (UNOC) import all petroleum products destined for the Ugandan market to ensure security of supply. However, some issues undermine this objective. The Company’s storage capacity at Jinja Storage Terminal (JST) is limited to 30 million litres, while the country’s average daily petroleum demand is approximately 6.5 million litres. UNOC has converted the JST facilities into a commercial hub to supply other marketing companies, with trade stocks averaging 5.2 to 7.5 million litres per month, essentially matching daily national consumption. This leaves no room for strategic buffer stocks. The limited storage capacity exposes the country to high risk from both external supply shocks and internal operational disruptions, potentially threatening national energy security. Management explained that UNOC is planning to construct an additional storage tank for PMS to bring the total capacity of the terminal to 40 million litres, which will cover only five days’ stock of the country’s demand. Plans are also under way to construct Kampala Storage Terminal (KST), with storage capacity of 240 million litres. This will bring the combined storage between JST and KST to 280 million litres sufficient to cover up to 40 days’ worth of the country’s daily consumption. The only challenge that will remain will be on how to finance the stockholding for the 40 days estimated at UGX.1.3Tn. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer to fast track the development of additional storage facilities and to continue engaging the relevant stakeholders to provide funding for the national strategic reserves. 2.1.4.3 Restrictions on vessel Size for importation of PMS Objective 3 of the Petroleum Supplies Act, Cap 163, is to facilitate the Uganda National Oil Company Limited to import all Petroleum Products, destined for the Ugandan market to guarantee security of supply of Petroleum Products in the country. From the review of management reports, I noted that Uganda faced restrictions on the delivery vessels sizes for PMS. These were capped at 58,000MT with a maximum 5% tolerance. Whereas UNOC would typically prefer larger vessels to meet market demand efficiently and enhance supply security. This restriction constrains the Company’s ability to leverage the operational and economic advantages of larger shipments. Management explained that the Company continues to engage the relevant stakeholders to lift vessel capacity restrictions especially for PMS deliveries and as a result, in November 2025, UNOC was allowed to deliver an additional 25,000 MT Vessel of PMS. 77 In addition, there are interventions by the Kenyan counter part stakeholders to allow UNOC to bring in the preferred vessel size of 85,000 MT from the current 58,000 MT which include; increasing the pumping rates from Mombasa to Nairobi and Western Kenya depots which will improve evacuation of fuel from Mombasa terminals; and enhancing the capacity of PMS storage in Western Kenya. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer to continue engaging the relevant stakeholders to negotiate for lifting of the vessel size restrictions and to explore alternative supply routes in order to enhance supply security and operational flexibility. 2.1.5 Sustainable Energy Development Programme 2.1.5.1 Uptake of available Generation Capacity In abid to achieve the Vision 2040 target of increasing Uganda’s generation capacity to 52,481Mw by 2040. In addition to Nalubaale-Kiira, Government constructed Karuma 600MW and Isimba 183MW using the on-lent loan from EXIM Bank of China of USD.1,398,516,759 and USD.567,738,990.96 respectively. A review of the quarterly operations and maintenance reports revealed that Nalubaale- Kiira power plant dispatched 778.8GWh (112%) against declared capacity of 695.6GWh, Isimba HPP had a Net energy output 1,046.41GWh(72%) against Declared available capacity of 1,451.06GWh and Karuma HHP had a net energy output of 808.27GWh(30%) against Declared available capacity of 2,652GWh. Further analysis indicates that in the first year of operation, Karuma HPP operated at an average of 70MWh and 116MWh in the second year which are below the minimum required dispatch of 300MW/h to enable the identification and addressing of the latent defects in generating units and associated plant structures, during the defects liability period. In addition, the company only realized UGX.148.16Bn (46.8%) out of the total expected revenue of UGX.316.42Bn.
