In the circumstances the company might not meet the loan and interest repayment terms/condition as well as operational and maintenance costs and ably identify defects before the expiry of the Defects liability period. Management attributed the low dispatch to inadequate demand for electricity and prioritization of low cost generating plants and private producers who are on capacity charge. UEGCL has engaged the regulator (ERA) and UETCL to allow for other players to buy the power from UEGCL and improvement of the export infrastructure respectively. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer of UEGCL to continue engagements with MEMD, ERA, UETCL and other relevant stakeholders to device mechanisms of increasing demand such as; 78 i) Promoting establishment of industrial parks and the corresponding connections. ii) Enhancing cross boarder power trade through the East African Power pool arrangement. iii) Expedite the electricity connections under the Electricity Access Scale Up Project. 2.1.5.2 Electricity Transmission Instruction 3.9.5 of the Treasury Instructions, 2017, requires budget estimates to be based on pre-determined objectives and outputs as provided in the strategic plans of the entity. Additionally, Instruction 16.9.1 mandates that the Accounting Officer prepare an annual budget for asset maintenance and systematically assess the performance of NCAs for functionality, utilization, and physical and financial performance. I noted the following; i) Multiple Independent Power Producers (IPPs) were unable to fully evacuate power during the period due to grid interruption events attributed to line faults, equipment failures, outages of transformers, vandalism incidents, SCADA limitations, and other transmission constraints. This resulted into deemed energy costs with a total of UGX.26.94Bn recognized as deemed energy obligations in the 4 quarters of the financial year. The persistence of these interruptions indicates ineffective utilization and reliability of key transmission assets, leading to avoidable financial obligations and increased operational costs. ii) I noted major transformers that have remained idle and out of service for extended periods without full restoration or replacement as shown in the table below; Table 31: Idle Transformers No Substati on Transformer Name Capacit y rating Last Used Idle Period Cause Action 1 Namanve 132/33 kV Tx 1 40 MVA 14/03/2023 27 months Inter-turn fault on Red-phase winding Decommissioned 2 Mutundwe 132/11 kV Tx 3 20 MVA 20/10/2024 8 months Fault on Blue-phase winding Installation of a 20MVA 33/11kV transformer 5 3 Lugazi 66/11 kV Tx 1 14 MVA 18/02/2022 40 months Faulty tap- changers Owen Falls-Lugazi transmission voltage was down rated from 66 kV to 33 kV and a step-down 60 MVA, 33/11 kV transformer installed at Lugazi. 4 Lugazi 66/11 kV Tx 2 14 MVA 20/01/2022 41 months Faulty tap- changers 5 Owen Falls 33/66 kV Tx 1 14 MVA 18/02/2022 40 months Bypassed to solve the Lugazi Issue 6 Owen Falls 33/66 kV Tx 2 14 MVA 18/02/2022 40 months 79 temporarily . 7 Agago 132/33 kV Tx 1 40 MVA New 11 months Lack of load Maintained on soak throughout. 8 Namanve South 132/33 kV Tx 1 63 MVA 10/07/2024 12 months Damaged 33kV switchgear Replacement of switchgear. Source: analysis of transformer data These long-term outages indicate non-utilisation of significant non-current assets and reliance on interim configurations, undermining optimal asset utilization and efficient delivery of transmission services. This implies a misalignment of NCAs with the company’s mandate, leading to inefficient service delivery and potential wastage of resources. Management explained that engagements with UEDCL are ongoing through monthly operations meetings to improve evacuation availability for embedded IPPs. Long-idle transformers are at different stages of resolution: irreparable units have been decommissioned and replacement procurements initiated; others are undergoing Original Equipment Manufacturer assessment, repair, or switchgear replacement, with some expected to be restored upon completion of related works. Certain transformers remain idle due to lack of load, which is expected to improve with demand growth. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer to urgently address the transmission constraints driving deemed energy costs and restore long-idle transformers through timely repair or replacement. A structured plan to improve asset availability, prevent recurring outages, and enhance evacuation capacity should be implemented to reduce avoidable financial losses and ensure optimal utilization of key transmission assets. 2.1.5.3 Electricity Distribution Following the expiry of UMEME’s concession on 31st March 2025, UEDCL assumed responsibility for a substantially expanded electricity distribution. By 30th June 2025, UEDCL’s asset base had grown from UGX.113Bn to UGX.2Tn, customers from 165,937 to 2.2Mn, staff from 480 to 2,489, and annual revenue from UGX.111Bn to UGX.661Bn, marking a significant operational and institutional scale-up. An assessment of UEDCL’s post-transition performance revealed service delivery challenges particularly in; network reliability, outage management, customer responsiveness, complaint resolution, and metering services. Management attributed the underperformance largely to a deteriorated network arising from prolonged underinvestment during the latter years of the concession, regulatory budget cuts, vandalism, electricity theft, procurement bottlenecks and staffing constraints. 80 Management further indicated that corrective interventions are being implemented and they include; the rollout of a loss-reduction strategy coined as the “Wetereze” campaign targeting commercial losses, enhanced field monitoring, and community enforcement activities as well as development of a five-year distribution network rehabilitation and investment plan , deployment of digital customer engagement platforms such as the “Social Media Integration and Digital Engagement Platform” and securing PPDA accreditation to ease procurement delays . In the meantime 39,996(50%) meters have been replaced since April 2025 against a backlog of 79,596 faulty meters. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer to implement a fully costed medium to long-term network rehabilitation plan, prioritize critical capacity upgrades particularly transformers and feeders in high-load areas, strengthen controls against vandalism and theft, and fully operationalize and leverage on procurement reforms to sustainably improve service delivery. 2.1.6 Agro-Industrialisation Programme 2.1.6.1 Delays to acquire land and establish a crude palm oil processing mill Government of Uganda, through the National Oil Palm Project is expected to acquire, compensate and hand over the 5,000 ha of land to Oil Palm Buvuma Limited (OPBL). The land was expected to have been acquired and handed over by Financial Year 2019/2020. In addition, OPBL was expected to construct a crude palm oil processing mill in Financial Year 2024/2025 to process fresh oil palm fruit harvested by farmers. I observed that; i) There was significant delay in compensating landowners by up to 17 months after the date of valuation, while in other cases land is yet to be compensated. Delayed valuation and compensation of PAPs may lead to increased compensation costs as a result of increase in the value of land over time. ii) By the end of the financial year 2024/2025, OPBL was yet to possess 629ha of land. Failure by government to provide the required acreage of land to OPBL may result in delays to fully establish the nucleus estate and attain the project objectives. iii) Out of the 4,371 ha that had been acquired and handed over, only 2,650.43ha had been cultivated. The failure by OPBL to cultivate the full acreage so far in their possession implies that the company may not have the capacity to fully cultivate the required land and establish the nucleus estate. iv) The crude palm oil processing mill was yet to be established by OPBL. Without a crude palm oil processing mill, farmers close to the nucleus estate may continue incurring costs of transporting fresh oil palm fruit from their gardens to Kalangala District for processing. v) The construction of crude palm oil processing mill was postponed by the investor from the earlier planned financial year 2024/2025 to the year 2027 with claims 81 that it was not a viable investment when still operating the nucleus plantation below 5,000 hectares. Recommendations I advised the Accounting Officer; i) To expedite the compensation of the project affected persons using the supplementary funds and ensure that the land acquired is put to immediate use for the project activities. ii) Once the target acreage has been achieved, OPBL should promptly establish the crude palm oil processing mill to enable farmers process their harvested fruit within Buvuma. iii) To establish the reasons why OPBL has failed to fully cultivate the land so far paid for and handed over. 2.1.6.2 Management of Agricultural Mechanisation Centres The Ministry has set up five (5) regional mechanisation centres in Buwama, Sanga, Kiryandongo, Agwata, and Bunghokho in addition to the National Mechanisation Referral Mechanisation Centre in Namalere to lease heavy farm equipment to farmers in the regions to increase their farm productivity, reduce reliance on labor, and improve efficiency in agricultural production. I reviewed the management of the regional mechanisation centres and noted the following; i) Lack of standard operating procedures/Guidelines; I noted that there were no operational guidelines to provide a framework for effective management and accountability for the mechanisation centres. As a result, the Ministry lacks guidance on the target groups, objectives of the interventions, the constitution of management committees and reporting among others. ii) Inadequacies in the management of the hiring of equipment to farmers; The mechanisms in place to account for equipment usage by farmers were inadequate, as there was no registers of requests for hire of equipment at each centre, or equipment logs to account for machine hours and services it has delivered. iii) Management of hired equipment; MAAIF lacks a standardised assessment criteria for identifying farmer beneficiaries to hire out equipment to. When equipment develops mechanical issues while hired out, there are no incident management reports showing the repair requirements and no logs showing the repair history of the equipment. iv) Revenue collection; There is no record of non-tax revenue generated from the hire of the equipment as no revenues could be traced to URA’s revenue collection records. v) Weaknesses observed at the Mechanisation centres; I observed that all the six (6) centres did not maintain sufficient records of their operations. Some 82 of the centres did not have proper offices from which the staff can operate, and the offices lacked computers and furniture. They were not equipped with repair workshops and equipment service bays. The Accounting Officer explained that the Ministry is developing a mechanisation policy to guide the management of the centres. Further, management has engaged MoFPED to increase the budgetary allocation to support the mechanisation centres to enable their efficient operation. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer to fast-track the development and approval of a mechanisation policy to streamline the management of the mechanisation centres. In addition, I advised the Accounting Officer to develop mechanisms to enhance the tracking of the hiring, deployment, use and maintenance of the mechanisation equipment. 2.1.7 Administration of Justice Programme 2.1.7.1 Growing case backlog at the Tax Appeals Tribunal Section 20(3) of the Tax Appeals Tribunal (TAT) (Amendment) Cap 341, provides that a decision on an application for review shall be made as soon as is practicable after the hearing has been completed; and the tribunal shall cause a copy of its decision, including the reasons for the decision, to be served on each party to the proceeding. The Tax Appeals Tribunal is facing a rapidly growing and high-value backlog of tax cases due to weak case disposal capacity, prolonged delays, and limited public awareness of its mandate. The average resolution time was 10 months, as summarized in the case ageing table below; Table 32: Age analysis of tax appeal cases SN Cases Ageing (Months) Number of Cases Amount (UGX-Bn) 1 10 to 20 119 442.5 2 20-30 30 201.7 3 30-40 27 33.002 4 40-50 1 0.004 5 50-60 1 6.463 6 >60 1 10.288 Total 179 693.957 Source: OAG analysis of case register As a result of delays in resolution shown above, the pending cases have risen from 169 in FY 2022/23 to 476 in FY 2024/25 and the value of unresolved disputes stands at UGX.1.5Tn. Management explained that the growing backlog was occasioned by the insufficient budget; despite the increase in TAT membership from 5 to 9 members in 2022, the 83 budget has remained static at UGX.7.7Bn which is inadequate to support the tribunal’s increasing workload. Recommendation I advised the Tax Appeals Tribunal to liaise with the relevant stakeholders to strengthen its capacity for disposal of tax appeals. 2.1.8 Governance and Security Programme 2.1.8.1 Review of the operations in the DNA Central Laboratory The Directorate of Government Analytical Laboratory (DGAL) was established to provide scientific and forensic analytical services to support the administration of justice. During the last three (3) years, the demand for DNA paternity testing has increased while there has been a trend towards the reliance on forensic science to support investigations. I analysed the DNA services to assess how they are delivered, managed and reported on and observed the following; i) DGAL identified the establishment of a National Forensic DNA database as a flagship initiative in their Strategic Plan (2020/21–2024/25). However, by the end of FY 2024/25, DGAL had not established a National Forensic DNA Database and the DNA Information System. ii) DGAL’s DNA division suffers from insufficient laboratory workspace. The limited space allows only one (1) analyst to perform the required procedures at a time, as the available space does not allow multiple analysts to work concurrently on similar procedures. This constraint is leading to substantial delays in case processing. iii) In the last five (5) years, the DNA backlog have remained high. Year-end backlogs increased from 786 cases in FY 2020/21 to 923 cases in FY 2024/25, representing a 17% growth over the five (5) years. iv) The DNA laboratory has four (4) genetic analysers for processing DNA samples. However, one analyser was obsolete; another, designated for wildlife DNA analysis, was functional but rarely used; a third was frequently used but operated below capacity; and the fourth, installed in January 2025, had not yet been put to use, eight (8) months after procurement. The Accounting Officer attributed the challenges to funding gaps. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer to liaise with the relevant stakeholders, including MoFPED and MIA to mobilise resources and improve the operations of DNA laboratories. 84 2.1.8.2 Review of the operations in the central and regional laboratories DGAL operates a central and four (4) regional laboratories in Mbale, Gulu, Moroto and Mbarara. I assessed the operations of the regional laboratories and observed the following; i) The four (4) laboratories are not efficiently and effectively utilised. Only the Gulu Regional Laboratory was partially performing limited forensic biology analyses. The Mbale and Mbarara laboratories functioned only as exhibit collection and sub-sampling centres, while the Moroto laboratory remained non-operational. ii) The four (4) regional laboratories handled 503 cases, representing 8% of DGAL’s total workload of 6,109 cases. Gulu accounted for 22% (111 cases) while Mbale and Mbarara accounted for the remaining 78% (392 cases) of the total regional workload. iii) The headquarters laboratory conducted quarterly outreach visits to regional laboratories to collect exhibits and samples for analysis in Kampala. However, the limited frequency of these visits caused delayed case transfers and turnaround times exceeding the 30-day benchmark set in DGAL’s Strategic Plan. iv) The approved DGAL staff structure provides for 60 positions across the four (4) regional laboratories. As of 30th June 2025, only 28 positions had been filled, leaving a staffing gap of 32 positions (53%) including two (2) Assistant Commissioner roles responsible for overseeing the regional laboratories. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer to adopt a phased operationalization strategy for regional laboratories, prioritizing the recruitment of critical technical and managerial staff in line with the available funding. In the meantime, I advised management to review and increase the frequency of outreach visits to regional laboratories to ensure timely transfer of samples and exhibits. 2.1.8.3 Review of the online business registration by URSB URSB’s Online Business Registration System (OBRS) was developed to digitalise business registration and improve service delivery. Over three (3) years, URSB has invested UGX.6.49Bn to design, develop, and maintain the OBRS. The system was launched in December 2022. I reviewed the system and observed the following; i) I noted significant delays in the registration of company names. A review of four (4) services offered through the OBRS i.e. company name reservation, business name amendments, business name registration, and data updates showed that the Bureau did not consistently meet the approved turnaround times. 85 ii) I observed regular, recurring OBRS system downtime. Incident logs showed multiple system outages between August 2023 and September 2025 due to network failures, storage exhaustion, inadequate power backup, and human error. These outages prevented users from processing business registration applications. iii) I noted that historical business registration records provided to third parties through the OBRS contained unredacted personal information, including full dates of births of directors, proprietors, or subscribers. iv) Controls to prevent fraudulent registrations were inadequate. For instance, fraudulent entries such as forged signatures and unauthorized filings were only addressed when detected or reported. The system is unable to authenticate digital signatures or confirm that approvals are submitted by legitimate owners of companies. v) Although URSB began the ISO 9001:2015 certification process in August 2018 and committed to complete certification by 30th June 2024, the Bureau had not obtained the certification by the end of FY 2024/25, resulting in a delay of one (1) year. vi) The Bureau did not maintain a register of customer complaints for the OBRS, including details of complaint types, resolution timelines, or a mechanism for clients to track resolution outcomes. As a result, URSB cannot identify recurring issues, measure effectiveness in reducing repeat complaints, or assess timeliness of resolution of client complaints. Recommendations I advised the Accounting Officer to; i) Strengthen service availability and limit system downtime by monitoring storage, power, and network performance, and establishing redundancy for critical servers. ii) Implement data minimization and redaction controls for records shared with third parties. iii) Benchmark with other government institutions on safeguarding e-signatures and consider integrating digital signature authentication into OBRS. iv) Prioritise the full implementation of ISO 9001:2015 QMS requirements, including a comprehensive customer complaints management system. 2.1.8.4 Challenges in implementation of Security Interest in Movable Property Act Government introduced the Security Interest in Movable Property Act, Cap. 293 in 2019, to promote the use of movable assets as collateral for accessing credit to increase access to credit for Ugandans particularly women, youth, and low-income earners who do not own registered land, which is the preferred collateral for most lenders. 86 To support the initiative, URSB developed the Security Interest in Movable Property Registry System (SIMPRS) at a cost of UGX.1.2Bn to automate registration of security interests by licensed lenders, including SACCOs, Micro Finance Institutions, commercial banks, community-based organisations, and other authorised lenders. SIMPRS facilitates secured creditors and lenders to register their security interests in movable assets such as livestock, farm produce, motor vehicles, machinery, intellectual property, electronics, and household furniture while providing the public with notice of the existence of these interests. Once a lender registers a security interest, the borrower retains the interest until the debt is fully repaid. A review of the SIMPRS system revealed the following implementation challenges; i) Most movable assets eligible for registration under the Act, such as livestock, ICT equipment, household goods, and agricultural produce and tools lack unique identifiers making it difficult for lenders to reliably verify legal ownership, existence, or traceability of collateral. ii) The Ministry of Trade has no central registry for registering movable equipment entering Uganda’s borders, making assets identification and traceability difficult and increasing the likelihood that borrowers may use the same asset to secure credit from several lenders. iii) Although agricultural warehouse receipts have unique identifiers, URSB cannot authenticate them because the Warehouse Receipt System under the Ministry of Trade is not integrated with SIMPRS. As a result, lenders cannot verify the validity or value of pledged warehouse-stored commodities. iv) Only licensed lenders are allowed to register interest on the system however, due to the absence of integration with Uganda Microfinance Regulatory Authority, URSB cannot verify whether a user has an active or expired license in real time, exposing SIMPRS to misuse by unlicensed or deregistered lenders. v) SIMPRS has no mechanism to protect lenders from asset depreciation, loss, theft, or deterioration, and there are no linked insurance, guarantee, or risk- mitigation instruments. This gap increases lender exposure and contributes to the low uptake of SIMPRS, particularly for high-risk movable assets. vi) The Bureau has no mechanism in place to real time monitor and deregister or discharge interests where borrowers have fully settled their loans and only present active interests. Recommendations I advised the Accounting Officer to liaise with all the responsible stakeholders to; i) Introduce unique identifiers for key movable assets eligible for use as collateral in order for the system to work as intended. 87 ii) Establish a central registry for movable equipment crossing Uganda’s borders to address the risk of multiple pledging of assets. iii) Integrate the Warehouse Receipt System with SIMPRS to enable lenders verify the validity and value of pledged warehouse commodities. iv) Link SIMPRS with the Uganda Microfinance Regulatory Authority to verify in real time whether users are licensed. 2.1.8.5 Registration of Intellectual Property The Trademarks Act, Cap. 225 protects registered trademarks from unauthorized use, imitation, or passing-off, thereby safeguarding brand identity, service credibility, and government intellectual property. The Act further provides that a trademark shall be registered for a period of 14 years, with the option for renewal thereafter. I reviewed the trademarks register, records and related reports and observed the following; i) Out of a sample of 76 trademarks associated with various Government institutions, 56 were not registered, four (4) had expired, six (6) trademarks were pending publication, and only 10 trademarks were valid (properly registered) and active. ii) There is a significant gap between business registration and trademark uptake. Despite URSB having over 850,000 registered businesses, fewer than 11,000 local trademarks have been registered, implying that over 98% legally registered Ugandan companies have no trademarks and therefore lack commercial protection, leaving them vulnerable to counterfeiting and unfair competition. iii) I noted that the Bureau has insufficient in-house capacity for patent review, especially expertise to conduct substantive examinations in specialized fields such as pharmaceuticals, medicine, engineering, and biotechnology. Consequently, over the past three years, at least 56 applications that passed formality examination were referred to the African Regional Intellectual Property Organization (ARIPO) for substantive review, which takes five years or more compared to about two years locally. iv) The Bureau has not yet finalized the development of a National Policy on Business Formalisation to guide the national agenda, owing to limitations in mandate. The lack of which hinders the development of a coherent, multi- sectoral approach to addressing informality in Uganda, limiting efforts to enhance productivity and foster economic growth. Recommendations I advised the Accounting Officer to; i) Encourage more government institutions to register their trademarks. 88 ii) Promote increased trademark registration among businesses through awareness campaigns and streamlined processes for registration. iii) Building in-house capacity for patent examinations in specialized fields. iv) Complete the development of the National policy on Business Formalisation to provide a framework to guide the transition of informal businesses into formally registered businesses. 2.1.9 Regional Balance Development Programme 2.1.9.1 Limited involvement of the Diaspora in PDM activities The Parish Development Model (PDM) Pillar 1 requires government MDAs to organize and mobilize households and stakeholders, including the Ugandan diaspora, for production, processing, and marketing support. A review of the MoFA PDM Impact and Opportunities for the Ugandan Diaspora document, and interviews with MoFA officials revealed that; i) There were no diaspora needs assessments conducted to align diaspora interests with PDM priority value chains. ii) There is no structured mechanism for linking diaspora investors to processing plants/factories, storage facilities, or agribusiness ventures under PDM. As a result, the level of involvement of Ugandans in the diaspora in agricultural investments is low. iii) There was no evidence of diaspora mobilization for agricultural value chains under the PDM such as export markets, technology transfer, off-taker arrangements. iv) MoFA does not systematically collect or share diaspora agribusiness data with the PDM Pillar 1 Working Group. v) No reporting mechanism exists to capture or track diaspora contributions to PDM Pillar 1. This is due to failure by MoFA to prioritize and operationalize diaspora engagement within the PDM framework. Recommendations I advised the Accounting Officer to; i) Streamline PDM activities in its work plans and missions abroad. ii) Establish a mechanism to systematically capture and share data with all relevant stakeholders on implementation of PDM. 2.1.10 Public Sector Transformation Programme 2.1.10.1 Understaffing of the Uganda Public Service As at December 2024, the total approved establishment for Uganda’s Public Service stood at 658,104 positions, of which 356,504 were filled, translating into an overall 89 staffing level of 54% and a staffing gap of 301,600 positions (46%). The table below refers; Table 33: Understaffing of the Uganda Public Service SN Category Approved establishment Staff in Post’ Dec 2024 % of fill Staffing Gap % of Vacancies 1. Uganda Police Force 69,823 45,987 66% 23,836 34% 2. Teaching Service 268,615 173,219 64% 95,396 36% 3. Ministry’s & Departments 21,844 13,821 63% 8,023 37% 4. The staffing gaps were mainly attributed to inadequate wage provisions and expansion of staff structures, particularly in the health sector, without corresponding recruitment. The 54% staffing level means that nearly half of all public service positions remain unoccupied, hence negatively affecting quality and efficiency of service delivery. The Accounting Officer explained that the low staffing levels are mainly due to the phased filling of the newly adopted staffing structures for hospitals and health centres, as Government gradually strengthens hospital infrastructure. However, Government is prioritizing recruitment for the most urgent and critical vacancies. In addition, the Ministry has allocated additional wage resources to strengthen manpower and raise staffing levels. In FY 2025/2026, Uganda Police Force was allocated additional wage to recruit 10,000 constables, and Uganda Prisons Services to recruit 1,000 prison warders/wardresses. A total of 130 Ministries, Departments, Agencies, and Local Governments were cleared to recruit 6,749 employees with wage funding of UGX.122.38Bn and UGX.5.48Bn was allocated for newly upgraded Health Centre IIs to IIIs. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer to develop and publicise realistic multiyear recruitment plans aligned to the government’s wage projections and, in collaboration with MoFPED and the Public Service Commission (PSC), progressively fill the staffing gaps, prioritising the critical and high impact positions. 90 2.1.10.2 Rationalisation of Public Expenditure (RAPEX) On 22nd February, 2021, Cabinet approved the policy to merge, mainstream and rationalise various government entities to facilitate efficient and effective service delivery and eliminate mandate and functional overlaps. As of December 2025, 35 bills had been assented to for rationalisation of 40 entities. Out of the 40 entities, 23 entities had been successfully rationalised while 17 entities are yet to be rationalised. Of the 23 rationalised entities, 17 were mainstreamed and their functions transferred to successor entities, while six (6) were merged to form new entities. I carried out a detailed review of eight (8) rationalised entities and observed the following; a) Payment of terminal benefits following rationalisation At the time of writing this report, the following observations were noted; i) None of the eight (8) rationalised entities had specific budgets for the payment of rationalisation expenses (terminal benefits). Instead, their budgets were amalgamated under the successor MDAs. This implied that the individual entity budgets may not have been realistic. ii) As of the dates of closure, the eight (8) rationalised entities had 1,917 staff. Out of these, 1,492 staff (78%) were absorbed by other government entities, while the balance of 425 staff (22%) were not absorbed by any other government body. iii) Out of 1,492 staff absorbed by government entities, a total of 1,389 staff absorbed by seven (7) rationalised entities were paid UGX.46.80Bn as terminal benefits. This was inspite of the Attorney General’s Letter and RAPEX guidance by MoPS which provided that where an employee was re-appointed into government service, there would be no compensation, as this was considered continuity of service. iv) A total of 85 staff who were absorbed from five (5) entities were not paid terminal benefits. This implied that the absorbed staff were not entitled to terminal benefits. v) A total of 425 staff retired following the rationalisation exercise. Of these, 410 staff that had retired from six (6) entities had so far been paid terminal benefits amounting to UGX.30.4Bn, while 20 staff that had retired from two (2) entities had not been paid their terminal benefits. Similarly, a number of retired staff due to rationalisation from three (3) entities claimed UGX.2.08Bn. vi) A total of 66 staff were terminated from two (2) entities and entitled to terminal benefits of UGX.1.03Bn as provided for in their respective staff regulations, 91 contracts and human resources manuals. However, they were paid only UGX.930.11Mn leaving an unpaid balance of UGX.101.80Mn. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officers to bring the matters of ambiguity and inconsistencies in the guidance on terminal benefits, including varying interpretations by individual entities on who is entitled to receive terminal benefits, and the inconsistent computation of the benefits across RAPEX entities, to the attention of the Attorney General, the Ministry of Public Service and other relevant stakeholders for further guidance and final resolution. b) Review of assets and liabilities of the Rationalised Entities RAPEX guidelines required entities to prepare handover reports specifying the assets to be transferred to successor entities. At the time of writing this report, the following was observed; i) The assets in the handover reports of four (4) rationalised entities worth UGX.564.71Mn differed from those disclosed in the fixed assets register. Similarly, the assets of three (3) entities worth UGX.54.44Bn differed from those in the closure financial statements. ii) Twelve (12) assets valued at UGX.779Mn were left out of the handover reports of (1) entity at the time of the closure of the audit. iii) I circularised third parties and observed that seven (7) parcels of land whose values could not be established were not included in the handover reports as well as the financial statements of one (1) rationalised entity. iv) One (1) entity had carried out a Board of Survey to ascertain all the assets held at the time of closure, while seven (7) were yet to carry out the exercise as required by the RAPEX guidelines. v) Physical verification of the land owned at the rationalised entities revealed that 19 parcels of land in two (2) rationalised entities were encumbered, with 10 encroached on, while the ownership of seven (7) parcels of land is disputed. vi) 79 parcels of land that belonged to four (4) rationalised entities were not titled while five (5) parcels of land in one (1) rationalised entity had expired leases. vii) The total receivables of five (5) rationalised entities amounted to UGX.474.79Bn. viii) Five (5) rationalised entities had disclosed liabilities amounting to UGX.932.39Bn in their financial statements. This implied that Government is at a risk of loss of funds should the creditors sue before settlement of the liabilities. 92 Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officers of the successor entities to verify the assets before including them in their asset’s register and financial statements. I further advised Management in the successor entities to verify the liabilities before budgeting for their settlement. Where encumbrances on land were observed, management should take up the matter and ensure the prompt resolution. 2.1.10.3 Underutilization of Prime Land in Kenya Uganda Property Holdings Limited (UPHL) owns three large properties in Nyali, Kenya, a prime and commercially strategic location with strong potential for high-value development. However, physical inspection revealed that these properties, covering a combined four acres are currently leased to small, low-value tenants who generate minimal rental income relative to the land’s market potential. This underutilization limits UPHL’s ability to optimize revenue from its asset portfolio. Management reported that proposals for developing maisonettes and flats had been prepared and discussed with shareholders, but implementation stalled due to cash flow constraints. The continued underdevelopment of high-value land reduces the company’s earning capacity, weakens long-term financial sustainability, and delays opportunities for portfolio growth. Recommendation I advised UPHL Management to work with shareholders to mobilize the necessary investment resources and fast-track the development of these properties to maximize utilization and enhance revenue generation. 2.1.11 Climate Change, Natural Resources, Environment & Water Management Programme 2.1.11.1 Wetland Encroachment Contrary to Section 53(2) of the National Environment Act Cap 181 and Regulations 29(1) and 30(1) of the National Environment (Wetlands, Riverbanks and Lakeshores Management) Regulations 2000 requiring 100 meters and 200 meters protected zones from highest watermarks of rivers and lakes respectively, and Regulation 10(8) requiring five-yearly wetland inventory updates; i) Out of Uganda's wetlands cover of 33,762.6km² The total degraded wetland cover was estimated at 6.3% of Uganda’s total land area2. ii) Fourteen major water bodies suffered extensive encroachment; through apartment construction, hotels, sand mining, landing sites, washing bays, recreation facilities, wastewater discharge, sugarcane plantations, agriculture, settlements, quarrying, livestock grazing, cultivation, artisanal mining, brick- 2 Paragraph 293 of the NDPIV, Page 173 93 making, informal markets, unregulated water abstraction, rice farming, palm cultivation, charcoal production, illegal logging, and wetland drainage, among others3. iii) Despite restoration efforts, the Ministry of Water and Environment demarcated only 739.34km² (18%) against planned 4,150km² over three years4. iv) Whereas the National Environmental Management Authority issued 319 restoration orders in 2024/25, only 146 (46%) were acted upon leaving 173 (54%) orders pending5. The inadequate performance was attributed to limited funding whereby the Ministry received only UGX.660 Mn (11%) of the required funding of UGX.6Bn for demarcation of wetlands, absence of formal appeals regulations and guidelines and irregular sittings of the appeals committee. In addition, the ministry lacks command and control over the environmental police which also has only 45 officers responsible for protecting 8,614 gazetted wetlands covering approximately 37,346.3 km² across 146 districts and 11 cities6. The encroachment has led to; physical, chemical, and biological contamination manifesting as sedimentation, algal blooms, flash floods, rising water levels, reduced water quality, increased treatment costs, endangered aquatic biodiversity, compromised ecosystem services and public health risks. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer to liaise with Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development for necessary resources to enable buffer zone demarcation with concrete pillars, restoration of degraded areas, recruitment and control over the environmental police, and proactive coordination with NEMA and Local Governments regarding water banks and wetlands protection. 2.1.11.2 Maintenance of Valley Tanks and Dams in the Karamoja Sub-Region The Ministry of Water and Environment (MWE) and the Office of the Prime Minister, constructed 106 valley tanks at an estimated cost of UGX.8.7Bn and five dams at an estimated cost of UGX 45Bn across nine (9) districts in the Karamoja Sub-Region to support livestock, irrigation, and domestic water use. Upon completion, the infrastructure was handed over to communities through Water User Committees responsible for operation, management, and maintenance. During the year under review, the Ministry of Water and Environment received the budgeted UGX 1Bn for maintenance of 10 valley tanks and UGX100Mn for the rehabilitation of 3 of dams7. 3 Interview with the Commissioner, International Transboundary Water Affairs 4 Wetlands Performance Reports, and interviews with the senior wetlands officer 5 NEMA annual performance reports FYs 2022 to 2025 6 Interview with the commandant, environmental protection police unit 7 Water for production, Karamoja Work Plan 94 However, inspections of twenty-five valley tanks and five dams conducted in November 2025 revealed that eighteen valley tanks (72%) were heavily silted, while seven (28%), had maintenance challenges, including eroded water inlets, weed invasion, unprotected water sources, damaged animal drinking troughs, dilapidated cattle access ramps, and eroded embankments. Of the five dams inspected, three (60%) were well maintained, one (20%) had maintenance gaps such as overgrown grass and damaged animal drinking troughs, and one dam at Kawomeri was non-functional due to lack of water, attributed to encroachment of the catchment area. Consequently, the silted valley tanks and dams have suffered reduced water storage capacity, resulting in limited water availability for livestock and agriculture. This condition was attributed to the absence of clear maintenance plans, unclear roles between Local Governments and the Ministry of Water and Environment, limited community ownership, inadequate practical training of Water User Committees and community members in operation, maintenance, and water source protection, unprotected catchment areas leading to degradation, and overgrazing due to high livestock numbers, particularly affecting valley tanks. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officer to establish clear maintenance plans and budgets for all the 106 valley tanks and 5 dams, clarify the roles of Local Governments and the Ministry of Water and Environment, protect water sources through reforestation, and provide Water User Committees and community members with practical training in operation and maintenance, basic repair skills, and water source protection techniques. 2.1.12 Development Plan Implementation Programme 2.1.12.1 Low Tax/GDP ratio According to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), developing countries should maintain a Tax-to-GDP Ratio of at least 15% to ensure they have the funds to invest in the future and achieve sustainable economic growth. Tax-to-GDP Ratio represents total tax revenue as a percentage of GDP and indicates the share of a Country's output that the Government collects through taxes. I noted that although URA’s efforts have yielded impressive results with a tremendous growth in revenue collection, Uganda's Tax/GDP Ratio has remained low at around 13.4%. A comparison of Uganda’s performance with other economies revealed wide disparities, as shown in the table below; Table 34: Uganda's performance compared to other economies Particulars Tax/GDP ratio Uganda 13.4% Recommended for Developing Countries 15% World Average 23% Sub-Saharan Africa Average 18.6% OECD Average 34% Source: IMF database 95 From the above analysis, it is clear that Uganda has continued to perform on a lower scale compared to other countries in the region and globally. A critical analysis of the issue revealed structural imbalances between economic activity and tax revenue generation, with agriculture making a significant contribution to GDP but relatively little contribution to tax revenues. Government tax revenue remains heavily concentrated in trade and manufacturing sectors, as demonstrated in the table below; Table 35: Analysis of various sectors’ contribution to Tax and GDP over two years SN Current Sector Main Activity % Contribution to Taxes % Contribution to GDP FY 2023/24 FY 2024/25 FY 2023/24 FY 2024/25 1 Agriculture, forestry and fishing 0.80 1.63 24.6 26.1 2 Mining and quarrying 1.64 2.17 1.3 1.2 3 Manufacturing 21.79 22.19 15.1 14.5 4 Real estate activities 2.43 2.53 6.0 5.7 5 Education 1.77 1.67 3.6 3.6 6 Human health and social work activities 2.10 1.94 3.2 3.0 Source: OAG analysis of sector contributions to GDP/Tax The imbalance is mainly attributed to the current Tax Policy and residual inefficiencies in tax administration. Consequently the tax base has remained narrow without headway in taxing all potential sources, hence the debt dependency to bridge the financing gap. Recommendation I urged Government to revisit the Tax policy and improve the tax administration aspect to align the tax collection with the contribution to GDP. 2.1.12.2 Public Debt The total public debt has increased from UGX.69.20Tn in June 2021 to UGX.114.60Tn in June 2025, representing a growth of approximately 65.6% in 5 years. The table below refers. Table 36: Government Debt Financial year ended Domestic debt (UGX Tn) Foreign debt (UGX Tn) Total (UGX Tn) % Change June 2025 59.019 55.585 114.604 22.43 June 2024 39.159 54.449 93.608 9.30 June 2023 33.168 52.472 85.640 9.95 June 2022 29.425 48.463 77.888 12.55 June 2021 24.889 44.313 69.202 - Source: OAG analysis of public debt database From the table above, I noted a shift towards domestic financing to bridge budget shortfalls as domestic debt increased from UGX.39.16Tn in June 2024 to UGX.59.02Tn in 96 June 2025, surpassing external debt and raising its share of the total portfolio to 51.50% for the period under review from 41.83% in the prior FY 2023/24. I analysed the sovereign credit ratings to assess the Government’s ability to repay its public debt both in principal and in interest on time and noted as below; i) Although there was a rise in the Public Debt to GDP Ratio from 45.95% in 2023/24 to 50.29% in 2024/25. The indicator still remains below the set target of 54% implying that in projection Government can still service its debt without distress. ii) The Domestic debt interest payments to total revenues Ratio increased from 21% the previous year to 23.66%. It was noted that this was not converging towards the National Charter for Fiscal Responsibility benchmark of 12.5%. I however, noted that this sharp rise was a one off transaction where Government entered into an agreement with BoU to issue a 10-year amortized government bond amounting to UGX.7.779Tn in respect of outstanding funds borrowed to finance the budget during CoVID 19 pandemic. Recommendation I urged the PS/ST to keep the public debt under watch. 2.1.12.3 Domestic Arrears A review of the Consolidated Financial Statements of the Government of Uganda and the disclosure in Note 25 revealed that the GoU had accumulated domestic arrears to a tune of UGX.8.4Tn as at 30th June 2025, a reduction of 39% from prior year arrears of UGX.13.814Tn. This office is conducting a comprehensive verification of the domestic arrears across all Ministries, Departments, Agencies, and Local Authorities. The objective is to determine the accurate stock of domestic arrears for the Government. Detailed procedures have been designed to ensure that the Government's position on domestic arrears is accurately reflected. The detailed findings will be published separately. Recommendation I advised the PS/ST to ensure adequate budgeting for domestic arrears and enhance enforcement of commitment control for sustainability. 2.1.12.3.1 Gaps in taxation of digital services allow non-resident companies to earn from Uganda without paying taxes Global trade has shifted toward digital platforms offering entertainment, advertising, software subscriptions, cloud services, online education, and betting services. These services generate substantial income from Ugandan consumers, much of which flows to non-resident companies outside Uganda’s tax jurisdiction. 97 To tax this fast-growing sector, a 5% Digital Service Tax (DST) was introduced in FY 2023/24. Uganda collected UGX.29.58 billion in FY 2024/25 from 82 compliant providers through DST and VAT. However, my review revealed major providers that are not registered for DST and are not paying taxes on income earned from Ugandan users. This means Uganda is losing revenue to some of the world’s most profitable digital multinational companies. URA currently lacks a payment gateway monitoring system, making it difficult to quantify how much income these companies earn from Uganda, further limiting enforcement. Management explained that many of the non-compliant companies are based in the United States, which strongly resists DST regimes imposed by foreign countries. Recommendation I advised Management to ensure stronger tools and international cooperation, to minimise losses of billions in tax revenue from the fast-growing digital services. 2.1.12.3.2 Persistent delays in cargo and motor vehicle clearance increasing the cost of doing business The ASYCUDA-based clearance system operated by URA is meant to streamline import clearance by integrating UNBS, NDA, MAAIF, MOWT, UCDA, and other agencies into a single coordinated process, with a target of 3 days in which clearance should be completed. However, traders consistently reported delays in cargo and motor vehicle clearance. To validate the complaints, I analysed 973,336 entries handled by all regulators during FY 2024/25. The table below illustrates the delays by the various agencies; Table 37: Cargo clearance delays of selected Agencies No Agency Average Clearance Time 1 MAAIF – Crop 36 days 2 MAAIF – Fish 25 days 3 UNBS 6 days 4 MOWT 9 days 5 NDA 4 days Source: URA Asycuda These delays are caused by repeated inspection steps, slow processes at various entities, and client non-compliance with Pre-Export Verification of Conformity (PVoC). This has led to; i) Increased cost of doing business 98 ii) Longer turnaround time for importers iii) Accumulation of cargo at the border iv) Reduced competitiveness of Uganda’s trade environment Management acknowledged that delays often originate from client failure to complete PVoC, limited awareness among SMEs, and the need for multiple regulatory checks. Recommendation I advised URA to streamline processes and harmonise the operations of the various agencies to eliminate clearance inefficiencies that harm the business environment and Uganda’s competitiveness. 2.1.12.4 Revenue performance by URA I undertook a trend analysis of revenue collected in the last four financial years and noted that collections have significantly increased over the last four years from UGX.22,098Bn in FY 2021/22 to UGX.32,357Bn in FY 2024/25. Table 38: Total URA collected revenues for the past four financial years Revenue Category Amounts (UGX Bn) ) FY 2024/25 FY 2023/24 FY 2022/23 FY 2021/22 Customs and Excise Taxes 9,604 8,160 7,711 6,755 Value Added Tax 8,779 7,800 7,291 6,452 Taxes on Gains, Profits, Fees and Licenses 11,943 10,221 9,151 7,578 Non-Tax Revenue 1,765 1,573 1,471 1,229 Petroleum Revenue 264 184 124 81 Total Gross Revenue Collections 32,357 27,938 25,751 22,098 Source: URA Revenue audited financial statements The significant growth in revenue has mainly arisen from Taxes on Gains, Profits, Fees and Licenses, Value Added Tax, as well as Customs and Excise Taxes. The upward trend in revenue collections is partly attributed to improved tax administration by the Uganda revenue Authority, through the introduction of solutions like the Electronic Fiscal Receipting and Invoicing Solution (EFRIS), as well as the Digital Tax Stamps (DTS), which have increased compliance levels among the taxpayers. Recommendation I urged Management to continue embracing innovations in tax administration for improved revenue performance. 2.1.12.5 Contribution of the EFRIS to Domestic Revenue Collection Uganda Revenue Authority (URA) introduced the Electronic Fiscal Receipting and Invoicing Solution (EFRIS) to digitise tax reporting, combat fraud (like invoice trading), and boost revenue by tracking all business transactions in real-time through mandatory 99 e-invoices/receipts, moving businesses from paper invoices to electronic invoices, aiming for transparency and wider tax base inclusion. The system was introduced in FY 2020/21 and initially mandatory for only VAT- registered taxpayers. Effective July 2025, it was expanded to include other businesses (even non-VAT registered ones) operating within specific sectors, which include wholesale and retail of fuel, real estate, construction, and manufacturing, among others. A review of the VAT revenue collections indicates slow growth before the introduction of EFRIS in the years 2017/18, 2018/19 and 2019/20, while a significant growth has been registered over the 5 years of implementation of the system, as indicated in the table below; Table 39: VAT collection trends over eight years Financial Year VAT Revenue Collections (UGX-Tn) Remarks FY 2024/25 8.780 Revenue collections after implementation of EFRIS FY2023/24 7.800 FY 2022/23 7.292 FY 2021/22 6.452 FY 2020/21 5.638 FY 2019/20 5.010 Revenue collections before the implementation of EFRIS FY 2018/19 5.125 FY 2017/18 4.581 Source: OAG analysis of URA VAT revenue collection The above analysis implies that EFRIS has been pivotal to the increased VAT revenue collections. Whereas the system has been majorly implemented for VAT, it has tremendously impacted performance in other tax heads, such as Income Tax, since the information therein is used to confirm taxpayer declarations made in other tax heads, such as Income Tax and Withholding Tax. The plans to extend EFRIS to other sectors is a plausible idea as it is expected to impact revenue collections across the country. 2.1.12.6 Low proportion of revenue contributing taxpayers I reviewed the total tax register which had 5,252,874 registered taxpayers as at 30th June 2025 and noted that only 2,524,666 (48%) had contributed some revenue during the financial year. This implies at 52% of the registered taxpayers had not contributed any revenue to the Authority. Table 40: Proportion of revenue contributing taxpayers Category Total Register Taxpayers that contributed %age of Value Taxpayers Total Register 5,251,874 2,524,666 48% Source: OAG analysis of URA tax register 100 It should further be noted that 1,076,846 (20%) of the contributing taxpayers, were employees whose collections were withheld by their employers. The low proportion of revenue-contributing taxpayers indicates that the taxpayer register contains a significant number of inactive or non-compliant taxpayers. This frustrates the effectiveness of registration initiatives and suggests that the Authority is not fully leveraging the growing taxpayer base to enhance revenue mobilization. The finding also implies that a relatively small proportion of taxpayers shoulder the revenue burden, which may lead to inequitable taxation, taxpayer fatigue, and reduced voluntary compliance. Management noted that the Taxpayer Register Management (TRM) is already executing a Register Cleaning project aimed at converting non-value taxpayers into value taxpayers by engaging them to file returns and pay the taxes due. They also noted that those established to be no longer eligible for registration are consequently deactivated from the register which will enable URA to maintain a register of only active taxpayers that are adding value and this is expected to be achieved by 30th June 2026. Recommendation I advised URA Management to; i) Conduct a comprehensive validation of the taxpayer register to identify inactive, duplicate, or non-operational taxpayers. ii) Develop and implement targeted compliance programs to activate dormant taxpayers and encourage newly registered entities to begin filing and paying taxes. 2.1.12.6.1 Operational challenges and conflicting laws in the regulation of the Microfinance sector a) Failure to operationalize the Stabilization Fund Section 53 and 56 (1) of the Tier 4 Microfinance Institutions and Money Lenders Act Cap 61 establishes a SACCO Stabilization fund and SACCO Saving Protection Fund respectively, and these are to be managed by the Uganda Micro Finance Regulatory Authority. These were intended to provide a safety net for SACCO members against SACCOs that have closed. However, the respective funds have not been operationalized as required due to the failure to approve the respective regulations. In addition, SACCOs have found the requirement to contribute 0.5% of the average total assets to the SACCO Stabilization Fund to be prohibitive. This exposes the 220 SACCO members to risks of loss in the event of collapse of a SACCO. 101 b) Conflicting laws There are various overlapping and conflicting laws between the Cooperatives Society Act and the Tier 4 Act in regard to: the use of the word SACCO, regulation and supervision, reporting of SACCOs and the Establishment of the SACCO Stabilization Fund and the Central Financing Facility, Liquidation of SACCOs and SACCO governance. For example, on the unclaimed balances, while ‘the Tier 4 Act provides that, unclaimed balances shall, after a period of 5 years be transferred to the Regulator for further management, the Cooperative Act provides that ‘the abandoned funds be credited to a special reserve fund thus the conflicting legal framework and overlapping laws causing a challenge in regulating SACCOs and encourage noncompliance issues in implementation. Recommendations I advised the Government to; i) Expedite the process of approving the regulations to operationalize the respective funds. ii) Ensure that the Tier 4 Microfinance and Money Lenders (SACCO) Regulations 2020 and the Cooperative Society Act are harmonised. 2.1.12.7 Compensations for the Kiteezi mud slide disaster victims On 10th August 2024, the Kiteezi waste slide occurred affecting over 230 residents of Kiteezi in Lusanja – Kansagati Town Council whose properties were destroyed. All of the affected persons were to be compensated through KCCA and OPM. Government released a total sum of OPM UGX.1.37Bn for the purpose while UGX.2.21Bn was the total claim under KCCA as valued by the Chief Government Valuer to be paid out. This amount was never released. However, at the time of writing this report, none of the claimants under KCCA had been compensated and under KCCA while 20 claimants under OPM have so far been compensated a total sum of UGX.1.05Bn. The failure to compensate all affected categories of victims has prolonged the suffering of households, whose livelihoods, homes, and properties were destroyed, leading to continued social and economic distress. The Accounting Officers of KCCA and OPM attributed the delay to the need for Cabinet approval and delays in securing the necessary funding. The funds have since been processed resulting in the payment of 70 out of the 95 affected beneficiaries under KCCA while the process of payment of disturbance allowance for the twenty (20) households under OPM is also ongoing. Recommendation I advised the Accounting Officers to expedite payment of the remaining 25 beneficiaries under KCCA and disturbance allowance to the 20 beneficiaries under OPM. In addition, a
